requirements.statement: Forward stepwise selection starts with the intercept-only model and at each step adds the one predictor that most improves the fit (highest R-squared among models with one more predictor), keeping previously selected predictors, giving one model per size; the final model is chosen across sizes by a criterion such as AIC.

places.quote: Efficient computation formula: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - \mu^2$ where $\mu = E[X]$
The second central moment is the [[Variance]], $\mu_2 = E[X^2] - \mu^2$.

requirements.statement: The maximum likelihood estimate is the parameter value that maximizes the likelihood (equivalently the log-likelihood) of the observed data.

places.quote: **Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)** is a method of parameter estimation that chooses the parameter value $\hat{\theta}$ that **maximizes the likelihood function** — the joint probability (discrete data) or joint density (continuous data) of the observed sample, read as a function of the parameter.

requirements.statement: The score function is the first derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter.

places.quote: When the maximum is at an interior point and the log-likelihood is differentiable, the MLE solves the **score equation** $\ell'(\hat{\theta}) = 0$.

requirements.statement: The MLE is found where the score function equals zero, so a plot of the score against the parameter crosses zero at the MLE.

places.quote: When the maximum is at an interior point and the log-likelihood is differentiable, the MLE solves the **score equation** $\ell'(\hat{\theta}) = 0$.
Taking the log and differentiating: $\ell(\theta) = -2\ln\theta - 9/\theta$; $\ell'(\theta) = -2/\theta + 9/\theta^2 = 0$ gives $\hat{\theta} = 9/2 = 4.5$.

requirements.statement: The deviance is minimized at the maximum likelihood estimate, so the minimum of a deviance plot locates the MLE.

places.quote: $$D^* = 2\left[\ell_{\text{sat}} - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right] = 2\left[\ell(\text{saturated model}) - \ell(\text{fitted model})\right]$$

requirements.statement: Fisher information measures the curvature of the log-likelihood (the precision of the estimate), being the negative expected second derivative of the log-likelihood.

places.quote: **Fisher Information** $I(\theta)$ measures how sharply the likelihood identifies a parameter — the expected curvature of the log-likelihood at $\theta$.
$$I(\theta) = -E\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\ln f(X \mid \theta)\right]$$

requirements.statement: The information function does not have a special feature (such as a zero or extremum) at the MLE, so it cannot be used to locate the MLE visually.

resolution.quote: measures how sharply the likelihood identifies a parameter — the expected curvature of the log-likelihood
resolution.note: passage on Fisher Information: information is the curvature of the log-likelihood, i.e. the precision of the estimate, not the location of its maximum (unlike the score's zero or the deviance's minimum); the check's miss.

requirements.statement: The failure rate (hazard rate) h(t) is the density divided by the survival function, f(t)/S(t), the instantaneous rate of failure at age t given survival to t.

places.quote: The **Hazard Rate** $\mu(t)$ (also called the **force of mortality** in life contingencies, or the **failure rate** in reliability) is the instantaneous rate of failure at time $t$ given survival to $t$.

requirements.statement: An exponential distribution has a constant hazard rate equal to the reciprocal of its mean (1/θ, i.e. the rate λ), independent of age.

places.quote: A **constant** hazard rate $\mu(t) = \mu$ corresponds to the [[Exponential Distribution|Exponential]] distribution: $S(t) = e^{-\mu t}$
Some texts parameterize by **rate** $\lambda = 1/\theta$, so $f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ and $E[X] = 1/\lambda$.

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: conditional on survival to age t, the remaining lifetime has the same exponential distribution, so past survival does not change the failure rate.

places.quote: Its defining property is **memorylessness**: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$, making it the unique continuous distribution with no aging effect
A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.

requirements.statement: The waiting time until the first event of a Poisson process with rate lambda is exponentially distributed with rate lambda (mean 1/lambda).

places.quote: Interarrival times $T_1, T_2, \ldots$ are i.i.d. $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ with mean $1/\lambda$

requirements.statement: A constant hazard rate lambda corresponds to an exponential lifetime distribution with rate lambda and mean 1/lambda.

places.quote: A **constant** hazard rate $\mu(t) = \mu$ corresponds to the [[Exponential Distribution|Exponential]] distribution: $S(t) = e^{-\mu t}$

requirements.statement: A parallel system fails only when all components have failed, so its lifetime is the maximum of the component lifetimes (a series system's lifetime is the minimum).

places.quote: A $k$-out-of-$n$ system fails at the $(n-k+1)$-th component failure, an [[Order Statistics|order statistic]].
$P\bigl(X_{(n)} \le x\bigr) = F_1(x)\,F_2(x)\cdots F_n(x)$

requirements.statement: For any two random variables, max(X,Y) + min(X,Y) = X + Y, so E[max(X,Y)] = E[X] + E[Y] - E[min(X,Y)].

places.quote: Relationship: $T_{xy} + T_{\overline{xy}} = T_x + T_y$, so $\mathring{e}_{xy} + \mathring{e}_{\overline{xy}} = \mathring{e}_x + \mathring{e}_y$

requirements.statement: The minimum of independent exponential random variables is exponential with rate equal to the sum of the individual rates, so its mean is 1/(sum of rates).

places.quote: $P\bigl(X_{(1)} > x\bigr) = \bigl[1 - F_1(x)\bigr]\bigl[1 - F_2(x)\bigr]\cdots\bigl[1 - F_n(x)\bigr]$

requirements.statement: For an exponential random variable with mean θ, the survival function is Pr[X > x] = e^{-x/θ}.

places.quote: Work from the survival function $S(x) = e^{-x/\theta}$ rather than the CDF; almost every exponential question is a tail probability
$E[X] = \theta$, $\text{Var}(X) = \theta^2$, and $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/\theta}$

requirements.statement: With an ordinary deductible d, the insurer makes a payment on a loss only if the loss exceeds d, so the probability of a payment is the survival function Pr[X > d]; with no deductible, a payment is made whenever the loss is positive, with probability 1.

places.quote: If the loss $X$ is less than or equal to the deductible $d$, the insurer pays nothing; above $d$ it pays the excess $X - d$
A payment is triggered only when $X > 300$:

requirements.statement: A p% reduction in the probability of a payment means the new probability equals (1 - p) times the original probability.

requirements.statement: The number of functioning components among n independent components, each with the same reliability p, follows a Binomial(n, p) distribution.

places.quote: The **Binomial Distribution** $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ models the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each with probability of success $p$.

requirements.statement: A k-out-of-n system functions when at least k of its n components function, so its reliability is the probability that at least k components function.

places.quote: **$k$-out-of-$n$** (works if at least $k$ work): with equal $p$, $r = \sum_{i=k}^{n} \binom{n}{i} p^i (1-p)^{n-i}$, a [[Binomial Distribution|binomial]] tail.

requirements.statement: The binomial probability mass function is Pr[K = k] = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k), and a probability of at least k successes is the sum of these terms over k to n.

places.quote: $$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$$
$r = \sum_{i=k}^{n} \binom{n}{i} p^i (1-p)^{n-i}$

requirements.statement: A path set is a set of components whose functioning guarantees the system functions; a minimal path set is a path set that contains no proper subset that is also a path set.
requirements.concept: Minimal Path Sets and Cut Sets

places.quote: A **minimal path set** is a set of components whose working alone makes the system work, with no proper subset doing so; a **minimal cut set** is a set whose failure alone makes it fail, again minimal.

requirements.statement: A cut set is a set of components whose failure guarantees the system fails; a minimal cut set is a cut set that contains no proper subset that is also a cut set.
requirements.concept: Minimal Path Sets and Cut Sets

places.quote: a **minimal cut set** is a set whose failure alone makes it fail, again minimal.

requirements.statement: To find minimal path sets and minimal cut sets from a system diagram, identify the smallest sets of components whose working connects input to output (paths) and the smallest sets whose failure disconnects input from output (cuts).
requirements.concept: Minimal Path Sets and Cut Sets

places.quote: A **minimal path set** is a set of components whose working alone makes the system work, with no proper subset doing so; a **minimal cut set** is a set whose failure alone makes it fail, again minimal.
Minimal path sets are the pairs $\{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}$; minimal cut sets are also the pairs, since $n - k + 1 = 2$ failures bring it down.

requirements.statement: In the five-component bridge network, the minimal path sets are {1,5}, {2,4}, {1,3,4}, {2,3,5}, and the minimal cut sets are {1,2}, {4,5}, {1,3,4}, {2,3,5}.
A set that strictly contains a path set (or a cut set) is not minimal, so it cannot be a minimal path set (or minimal cut set).
requirements.concept: Minimal Path Sets and Cut Sets

places.quote: with no proper subset doing so

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution with the memoryless property.

places.quote: Its defining property is **memorylessness**: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$, making it the unique continuous distribution with no aging effect
The uniform is **not** memoryless — the exponential is the only continuous density that is.

requirements.statement: Memoryless property: for X > d, the conditional distribution of the excess X - d given X > d is the same as the distribution of X, i.e. Pr(X - d > y | X > d) = Pr(X > y).

places.quote: A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.

requirements.statement: With an ordinary deductible d, the payment per loss is X - d when X > d and zero otherwise; the payment per payment is the excess loss X - d conditional on X > d.

places.quote: If the loss $X$ is less than or equal to the deductible $d$, the insurer pays nothing; above $d$ it pays the excess $X - d$
In insurance terms, it is the expected payment per payment under an ordinary [[Deductible|deductible]] of $d$.

requirements.statement: For an exponential distribution with mean θ, the mean excess loss (mean residual life) at any deductible equals θ.

places.quote: So $E[X \mid X > d] = d + \theta$ and $E[(X-d)_+] = \theta e^{-d/\theta}$
The [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] has a constant mean excess, $e_X(d) = \theta$, because it is memoryless.

requirements.statement: Gambler's ruin models a player's fortune as a random walk with independent rounds in which the player gains 1 with probability p or loses 1 with probability q = 1 - p, ending when the fortune hits 0 or a target N (absorbing boundaries).

places.quote: On each independent play the gambler wins one unit with probability $p$ and loses one with probability $q = 1 - p$; starting with $i$ units and stopping at $0$ or $N$, the fortune is a [[Markov Chain]] with absorbing states $0$ and $N$, and $P_i$ is the probability of reaching $N$ first.

requirements.statement: In gambler's ruin with p ≠ q, the probability of reaching N before 0 starting from i is (1 - (q/p)^i) / (1 - (q/p)^N).

places.quote: $P_i = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1 - (q/p)^i}{1 - (q/p)^N} & p \neq \tfrac12 \\[10pt] \dfrac{i}{N} & p = \tfrac12 \end{cases}$

requirements.statement: In a two-player game where coins only transfer between the players, one player has no coins exactly when the other holds all the coins in play (total N = sum of both starting amounts), so one player's ruin probability equals the other's probability of reaching N.

places.quote: When two players holding $a$ and $b$ units play until one is broke, follow one player's fortune: $i = a$, $N = a + b$, and $p$ is that player's chance of winning a round.

requirements.statement: The annual level benefit premium for a fully discrete whole life insurance follows from the equivalence principle: P = (face amount) × A_x / ä_x.

places.quote: $$P = \frac{A_x}{\ddot{a}_x}$$
Setting $E[L_0]=0$ gives $P = S\,A_x/\ddot{a}_x$.

requirements.statement: The Illustrative Life Table assumes an interest rate of 6% and gives values of l_x, q_x, ä_x and 1000A_x by age, and its values are read from the table for the original-table premium.
To find the effect of switching mortality tables, compute the premium under each table and take the difference (new minus original).

requirements.statement: The number of deaths among a block of independent lives with the same death probability over a period is binomial with n equal to the number of lives and p equal to that death probability.

places.quote: The **Binomial Distribution** $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ models the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each with probability of success $p$.

requirements.statement: The probability that a life aged x dies within t years is tqx = 1 - l_{x+t}/l_x, computed from life table values of l.

places.quote: $$_{t}p_x = \frac{\ell_{x+t}}{\ell_x}, \qquad _{t}q_x = 1 - {}_{t}p_x = \frac{\ell_x - \ell_{x+t}}{\ell_x}$$

requirements.statement: For a Binomial(n, p) random variable, the mean is np and the variance is np(1-p).

places.quote: $E[X] = np$ and $\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$

requirements.statement: A normal-approximation confidence interval for a count is mean ± z·standard deviation, where for a two-sided confidence level C the critical value z is the (1+C)/2 percentile of the standard normal (e.g., 1.645 for 90%).

places.quote: $$\bar{X} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \qquad (\sigma \text{ known})$$
Inverted, it sets a fund: the total exceeded with probability $\alpha$ is about $n\mu + z_{1-\alpha}\,\sigma\sqrt{n}$, where $z_{1-\alpha}$ is the standard normal [[Percentile|percentile]].

requirements.statement: In a Poisson process with rate lambda, interarrival times are independent exponential random variables with mean 1/lambda.

places.quote: Interarrival times $T_1, T_2, \ldots$ are i.i.d. $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ with mean $1/\lambda$
T_n \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda), \qquad E[T_n] = \frac{1}{\lambda}

requirements.statement: The waiting time until the nth event of a Poisson process is the sum of n independent exponential interarrival times (a gamma distribution).

places.quote: The waiting time $S_n = T_1 + \cdots + T_n$ to the $n$-th event follows a [[Gamma]] distribution with shape $n$ and rate $\lambda$
S_n = T_1 + \cdots + T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)
The sum of $n$ independent $\text{Exp}(\theta)$ variables follows $\text{Gamma}(n, \theta)$

requirements.statement: The inversion method simulates a random variable by setting a U(0,1) draw u equal to the CDF F(x) and solving for x = F^{-1}(u).

places.quote: simulates a draw from a distribution with [[Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)|CDF]] $F$ by generating $U$ from a [[Uniform Continuous Distribution|Uniform]]$(0, 1)$ distribution and returning the value $x$ at which the CDF reaches $U$.

requirements.statement: The exponential CDF is F(x) = 1 - e^{-lambda x}, so an exponential variable is simulated as x = -ln(1-u)/lambda (equivalently -ln(u)/lambda since 1-u is also U(0,1)).

places.quote: If $U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)$ and $\theta > 0$, then $Y = -\theta \ln U$ is exponential with mean $\theta$
For an [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] with mean $\theta$, $x = -\theta \ln(1-u)$

requirements.statement: For a single-parameter Pareto distribution with shape α and scale θ (density αθ^α/x^(α+1) for x > θ), the mean is E[X] = αθ/(α−1) for α > 1.

places.quote: The mean is $E[X] = \frac{\alpha\theta}{\alpha - 1}$ for $\alpha > 1$
$$E[X^k] = \frac{\alpha\,\theta^k}{\alpha - k}, \quad k < \alpha$$

requirements.statement: An estimator is unbiased for a parameter if its expected value equals the true parameter value for every possible value of the parameter.

places.quote: An estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of a parameter $\theta$ is **unbiased** if its expected value equals the true parameter value for all $\theta$.

requirements.statement: The sample mean of n independent identically distributed observations has expected value equal to the mean of the underlying distribution, E[X̄] = E[X].

places.quote: The **sample mean** $\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i$ is an unbiased estimator of the population mean $\mu$
$$E[\bar{X}] = \mu, \qquad \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$$

requirements.statement: A minimum variance unbiased estimator (MVUE/UMVUE) is an unbiased estimator whose variance is no larger than that of any other unbiased estimator for every parameter value.

places.quote: **Minimum Variance** is a criterion for comparing estimators: among the [[Unbiasedness|unbiased]] estimators of a parameter, the one with the **smallest variance** is preferred

requirements.statement: The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem states that an unbiased estimator that is a function of a complete sufficient statistic is the unique MVUE.

places.quote: **Lehmann–Scheffé Theorem.** If $T$ is complete and sufficient and $\varphi(T)$ is unbiased for $\tau(\theta)$, then $\varphi(T)$ is the **uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator** (UMVUE, or MVUE)

requirements.statement: For a normal distribution with unknown mean and variance, (sum of x_i, sum of x_i^2) is a complete sufficient statistic, because the normal belongs to the exponential family.

places.quote: A **complete sufficient statistic** combined with the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem yields the **UMVUE** (uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator)

requirements.statement: The sample variance s^2 = (1/(n-1)) * sum (x_i - xbar)^2, with divisor n-1, is an unbiased estimator of the population variance, and for a normal sample it is the MVUE of sigma^2.

places.quote: Dividing the sum of squared deviations by $n - 1$ rather than $n$ makes it an [[Unbiasedness|unbiased]] estimator of the population variance $\sigma^2$.

requirements.statement: The sum of squared deviations from the sample mean equals sum x_i^2 minus n times xbar^2.

places.quote: The computing form $S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\left(\sum X_i^2 - n\bar{X}^2\right)$ is what exam problems usually need

requirements.statement: The method of moments estimates parameters by setting the theoretical raw moments E[X^k] equal to the corresponding sample raw moments (1/n)ΣX_i^k, using as many moments as there are parameters, and solving for the parameters.

places.quote: $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i^{\,r} = E[X^{\,r}], \qquad r = 1, 2, \ldots, k$$
With $k$ unknown parameters, the first $k$ moment equations are used.

requirements.statement: The second raw moment of a random variable is E[X^2] = Var(X) + (E[X])^2, so for a normal distribution E[X] = μ and E[X^2] = σ^2 + μ^2.

places.quote: Two conditions (two percentiles or tail probabilities, or one of them plus a moment such as $E[X^2] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2$) give two equations, solved together for both $\mu$ and $\sigma$

requirements.statement: The method of moments variance estimate uses divisor n (the second sample raw moment minus the squared sample mean), so it is not the unbiased sample variance with divisor n-1.

places.quote: $$\text{Var}(X) = E\left[(X - \mu)^2\right]$$

requirements.statement: A kernel-smoothed distribution estimate replaces each observed data point with a kernel distribution centered at that point, and the smoothed CDF is the average over the n observations of the kernel CDFs evaluated at x.

places.quote: $$\hat{F}(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} W\!\left(\frac{x - x_i}{b}\right)$$

requirements.statement: For a uniform kernel with bandwidth b, the kernel CDF for observation y_i at x is 0 for x < y_i - b, 1 for x > y_i + b, and (x - (y_i - b))/(2b) for x between y_i - b and y_i + b.

places.quote: Its CDF rises linearly, $W(u) = \frac{u + 1}{2}$ on $[-1, 1]$.

requirements.statement: A policy deductible produces left-truncated data: losses below the deductible are not observed, and the observed payment is the loss minus the deductible, conditioned on the loss exceeding the deductible.

places.quote: In insurance, **left-truncation** arises with deductibles: only losses exceeding the deductible $d$ are reported.
**Left truncation.** Losses below a deductible $d$ are never reported, so each reported loss is drawn from $X \mid X > d$ and contributes $f(x)/S(d)$.

requirements.statement: A policy limit (maximum payment) produces right-censored data: when the maximum is paid, the loss is known only to be at least that amount.

places.quote: - **Right-censoring**: true value exceeds $c$ (e.g., policy limit reached, study ends before claim settles)
**Right censoring.** A loss at or above the maximum covered loss is recorded only as "at least $u$", so it contributes $S(u)$.

**Censoring:** A limit right-censors the loss. The variable $X \wedge u$ has a point mass of $S(u)$ at $u$, and a claim recorded at the limit says only that the loss was at least $u$, which is why such a claim enters a likelihood as $S(u)$ (see [[Censoring]]).

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: given X > d, the excess X - d is exponential with the same mean, so the deductible does not change the distribution of the payment.

places.quote: A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.
Exponential losses are memoryless, so $f(x)/S(d) = \theta^{-1}e^{-(x-500)/\theta}$.

requirements.statement: Construct the likelihood for truncated and censored data: each uncensored observation contributes its density (divided by the survival function at the truncation point), and each censored observation contributes the survival function at the censoring point.

requirements.statement: For an exponential distribution with censored data, the MLE of the mean is the sum of all observed values (censored values at their censoring point, and excess over any deductible) divided by the number of uncensored observations.

places.quote: **Exponential shortcut.** For an [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] model with any mix of truncation and right censoring, $\hat\theta = \dfrac{\sum_i (x_i - d_i)}{\text{number of exact observations}}$, summing over *all* observations, censored ones included.

requirements.statement: Type I error is rejecting H0 when H0 is true; its probability is the size (significance level) α = Pr(X in critical region | H0).

places.quote: A **Type I Error** occurs when a [[Hypothesis Testing|hypothesis test]] incorrectly **rejects a true null hypothesis** $H_0$. It is also called a **false positive**.
$$\alpha = \text{Power}(\theta_0) = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true})$$

requirements.statement: The power of a test is the probability of rejecting H0 when H1 is true, i.e. Pr(X in critical region | H1).

places.quote: The **Power of a Test** is the probability it rejects the null hypothesis when the null is false — the chance of detecting a real effect.
**Power** $= 1 - \beta = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_1 \text{ true})$

requirements.statement: By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, the most powerful (best) critical region for a simple-vs-simple test at a given size consists of the points where the likelihood ratio f0(x)/f1(x) is smallest.

places.quote: reject $H_0$ where the likelihood ratio $L(\mathbf{x}) = f_0(\mathbf{x})/f_1(\mathbf{x})$ is small.

requirements.statement: Points where the alternative density is zero add Type I error without adding power, so they are excluded from the best critical region; where the likelihood ratio is constant, any subset of the needed probability mass is equally good.
For a uniform distribution on [a,b], the probability of a subset region is its length divided by (b − a), with density 1/(b − a).

places.quote: $$f(x) = \frac{1}{b - a}, \quad a < x < b$$

requirements.statement: Thinning a Poisson process by independently classifying each event into types yields independent Poisson processes for each type, with rate equal to the original rate times the type's probability.

places.quote: **Poisson Thinning** (splitting) is the result that if each event of a [[Poisson Process]] with rate $\lambda$ is independently classified as type 1 with probability $p$ and type 2 with probability $1-p$, the two type counts are themselves **independent** Poisson processes with rates $\lambda p$ and $\lambda(1-p)$.
A Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ **thinned** by probability $p$ produces a Poisson process with rate $\lambda p$

requirements.statement: The waiting time until the first event of a Poisson process with rate λ is exponential with mean 1/λ.

places.quote: Interarrival times $T_1, T_2, \ldots$ are i.i.d. $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ with mean $1/\lambda$
For a [[Poisson Process]] with rate $\lambda$, the interarrival times are independent and identically distributed [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] variables with mean $1/\lambda$

requirements.statement: In a Poisson process with independent event types, the type of the first event is independent of the time at which it occurs, so its type follows the type probabilities regardless of the wait.

places.quote: Competing risks: if two independent Poisson streams have rates $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, the wait for the first event of either is $\text{Exp}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)$, and it is of type 1 with probability $\lambda_1/(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)$
each event of the merged process came from stream $i$ with probability $\lambda_i/\lambda$, independently of the other events and of the event times.

requirements.statement: Expectation is linear, so the expected value of a sum or difference of random variables equals the sum or difference of their expectations, even when they are dependent.

$$E[(X - d)_+] = E[X] - E[X \wedge d]$$

requirements.statement: Expected total time equals the expected waiting time plus the expected ride time, where the expected ride time is the probability-weighted average of the ride times over the train types.

places.quote: Any quantity that is *linear* in the density — a probability, a mean, a second moment — can be found by computing it within each subpopulation and averaging.

requirements.statement: The Pearson chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic is Q = Σ (O − E)² / E, summing over categories, where O is the observed count and E is the expected count.

requirements.statement: A paired t-test reduces two matched samples to a single sample of within-pair differences and tests whether the mean difference equals zero.
The sample variance of the differences is s_d^2 = sum (d_i - dbar)^2 / (n - 1), with s_d its square root.

requirements.statement: The one-sample/paired t statistic is t = dbar / (s_d / sqrt(n)), which follows a t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom under H0.

places.quote: this is what makes the $t$-statistic $\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1}$ work
$\dfrac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t(n - 1)$
The block is for an upper-tailed test; a lower-tailed test rejects when $T \le c$ with $P(T \le c \mid H_0) = \alpha$

requirements.statement: For a one-sided alternative, orient the differences so the alternative is a mean difference greater than zero, and the rejection region/p-value is the upper tail of the t distribution.

places.quote: a one-sided $H_1: \theta > \theta_0$ uses one tail, a two-sided $H_1: \theta \ne \theta_0$ uses both
For a **one-sided** test at level $\alpha$, read the $2\alpha$ column.
The block is for an upper-tailed test; a lower-tailed test rejects when $T \le c$ with $P(T \le c \mid H_0) = \alpha$

requirements.statement: The p-value is the smallest significance level at which the null hypothesis would be rejected.

places.quote: It is the smallest $\alpha$ at which the observed data would reject $H_0$, which is why software reports it instead of a fixed accept/reject verdict

requirements.statement: Bound a p-value by comparing the test statistic with critical values from a t table at the given degrees of freedom and finding the tail probabilities that bracket it.

places.quote: the entry $c$ satisfies $P(|T| > c) = $ the column heading.
The evidence of higher severity is significant at 5% but not at 1%, which places the p-value between them (it is about $0.032$).

requirements.statement: The sum of independent gamma random variables sharing a common scale parameter is gamma with the same scale and shape equal to the sum of the individual shapes.

resolution.quote: The sum of independent gamma random variables sharing a common scale parameter is gamma with the same scale and shape equal to the sum of the shapes
resolution.note: written from Siegrist 5.8 The Gamma Distribution (sums with common scale), https://www.randomservices.org/random/special/Gamma.html; checked by g8-masi-check-A1-2026-10-30

requirements.statement: A gamma distribution with shape parameter 1 is an exponential distribution with mean equal to the scale parameter.

places.quote: Special cases: exponential ($\alpha = 1$) and chi-squared ($\alpha = n/2$, $\theta = 2$)

requirements.statement: For an exponential distribution with mean theta, the survival function is P(X > x) = e^{-x/theta}.

places.quote: Work from the survival function $S(x) = e^{-x/\theta}$ rather than the CDF; almost every exponential question is a tail probability

requirements.statement: The mean payment per payment (mean excess loss) with an ordinary deductible d is e(d) = E[X - d | X > d], used when losses below the deductible are not reported.

places.quote: The **Mean Excess Loss** $e_X(d)$ is the expected amount by which a loss exceeds $d$, given that it does exceed $d$.

resolution.quote: is the mean excess loss at $u$: $e(u) = \dfrac{E[X] - E[X \wedge u]}{1 - F(u)}$
resolution.note: passage on Limited Expected Value (linked from Deductible): the mean excess loss at the deductible, the per-payment mean; the check's miss.

requirements.statement: When losses below the deductible go unreported, the relevant payment average is conditional on a payment occurring (per-payment basis), not averaged over all losses (per-loss basis).

places.quote: The average of the reported claims estimates $E[X \mid X > d]$, not $E[X]$, so it is biased **upward** (only the larger claims are seen).
**Per payment, not per loss:** $e_X(d)$ averages over losses above $d$ only. The expected cost per loss is $e_X(d)\,S_X(d)$, which is smaller.

requirements.statement: For a lognormal(mu, sigma) loss, E[X | X > d] = exp(mu + sigma^2/2) * Phi(sigma - (ln d - mu)/sigma) / (1 - Phi((ln d - mu)/sigma)).

resolution.quote: E[X \mid X > d] = \frac{e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}\,\Phi\!\left(\sigma - \frac{\ln d - \mu}{\sigma}\right)}{1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln d - \mu}{\sigma}\right)}
resolution.note: written from SOA Tables for Exam C (Loss Models App. A) A.5.1.1 Lognormal, https://www.soa.org/globalassets/assets/files/edu/edu-2009-fall-exam-c-table.pdf; checked by g8-masi-check-A1-2026-10-30

requirements.statement: The lognormal mean is exp(mu + sigma^2/2), and Pr(X > d) = 1 - Phi((ln d - mu)/sigma).

places.quote: $$E[X] = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}$$ … $$F(x) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\ln x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Evaluate standard normal CDF probabilities Phi(z) by looking up values in the standard normal table.

places.quote: Its CDF has no closed form and is evaluated via the standard normal $Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma \sim N(0,1)$ using $\Phi$ tables
The recipe: identify $n$, compute $E[S_n] = n\mu$ and $\text{Var}(S_n) = n\sigma^2$ ([[Moments for Linear Combinations]]), standardise, look up $\Phi$.

requirements.statement: For a sample from U(0, θ), the likelihood θ^(-n) is decreasing in θ but requires θ ≥ every observation, so the maximum likelihood estimator of θ is the sample maximum.

places.quote: for $\text{Uniform}(0, \theta)$, $L(\theta) = \theta^{-n}$ on $\theta \ge \max x_i$ is decreasing, so $\hat{\theta} = \max X_i$, where $\ell'(\hat{\theta}) = -n/\hat{\theta} \ne 0$

requirements.statement: The CDF of the maximum of n iid random variables is the n-th power of the individual CDF, so for U(0, θ) Pr(X_(n) ≤ x) = (x/θ)^n and the density is n x^(n-1)/θ^n.

places.quote: $$P\bigl(X_{(n)} \le x\bigr) = F_1(x)\,F_2(x)\cdots F_n(x)$$
so, for example, $P(X_{(n)} \le x) = F(x)^n$.

requirements.statement: The expected value of the sample maximum of n iid U(0, θ) observations is nθ/(n+1).

places.quote: the MLE $\hat\theta = X_{(n)}$ for $\text{Uniform}(0,\theta)$ is biased low by $\theta/(n+1)$
For $X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(0,\theta)$, the MLE is $\hat\theta = X_{(n)}$ with $E[X_{(n)}] = \frac{n}{n+1}\theta$.

requirements.statement: The bias of an estimator is its expected value minus the true parameter value, E[θ̂] − θ.

places.quote: $$\text{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta] - \theta$$

requirements.statement: A logistic regression model specifies the log-odds ln(p/(1-p)) of the event as a linear combination of the predictors, η = β0 + β1x1 + ... + βkxk.

places.quote: $$\ln\!\left(\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p$$

requirements.statement: In logistic regression the probability of the event is p = 1/(1 + e^{-η}) = e^η/(1 + e^η), where η is the linear predictor.

A binary categorical predictor enters the linear predictor as an indicator variable: its coefficient is added when the level is present (value 1) and nothing is added for the baseline level (value 0).

places.quote: A categorical predictor with $k$ levels is represented using $k-1$ **indicator (dummy) variables**; the omitted level is the **reference level**, absorbed into the intercept (see [[Parameter Estimate Tables]])
The **reference level** of a categorical predictor is absorbed into the intercept; other levels are interpreted relative to it

requirements.statement: Because the logistic function is strictly increasing in η, a probability threshold p > c is equivalent to the linear predictor exceeding the log-odds of the threshold, η > ln(c/(1-c)).

resolution.note: algebra: inverting the logistic function turns a probability threshold into a linear-predictor threshold, a shortcut; computing p = 1/(1+e^{-eta}) for each client (r2) answers it on Logistic Regression.

requirements.statement: A GLM with as many linearly independent parameters as observations (a saturated model) reproduces every fitted value exactly on the link scale, so the linear predictor equals g(fitted mean) for each observation regardless of the link function.

places.quote: the saturated model, which has one parameter per record and fits perfectly ($D^* = 0$)

requirements.statement: In a GLM the link function g relates the mean to the linear predictor, g(μ) = η = Xβ, so the fitted mean is μ = g⁻¹(Xβ).

places.quote: connects the **expected value** of the response $\mu = E[Y]$ to the **linear predictor** $\eta = \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}$
3. **Link function**: $g(\mu_i) = \eta_i$ connects the mean to the linear predictor

requirements.statement: With a design matrix of intercept, two binary indicators and their product, the interaction coefficient measures the departure from additivity of the two variables' effects on the link scale, equal to g(μ_AB) − g(μ_A) − g(μ_B) + g(μ_neither).

places.quote: If $\beta_3 = 0$, the two predictors act **additively** on the link scale — no interaction

requirements.statement: The identity link gives g(μ)=μ, the inverse link gives g(μ)=1/μ, and the log link gives g(μ)=ln μ; under a log link effects are multiplicative, so a zero interaction corresponds to equal ratios (μ_AB·μ_neither = μ_A·μ_B).

places.quote: | Log | $\ln\mu$ | $e^\eta$ | Poisson (counts), Gamma (severity) |
allows multiplicative interpretation: a unit increase in $x_j$ multiplies $\mu$ by $e^{\beta_j}$
The **log link makes the model multiplicative**, so $e^{\beta}$ is a relativity

requirements.statement: A GLM with a canonical link function and an intercept has maximum-likelihood equations that force the fitted values to sum to the observed values, so the model is unbiased in aggregate and within each level of each categorical predictor.

places.quote: The cross-classified model's likelihood equations set every row total and every column total of fitted values equal to the observed total.
Its maximum likelihood equations equate each row sum and each column sum of fitted values with the actual ones

requirements.statement: The canonical link of an exponential-family distribution is the link function that equals the natural parameter as a function of the mean (e.g., log for Poisson, inverse for gamma, identity for normal).

places.quote: The **canonical link** is the natural link arising from the exponential family form of the distribution
The **canonical [[Link Function]]** is the one with $g(\mu) = \theta$

requirements.statement: The canonical link for the Poisson distribution is the log link, while the gamma canonical link is the inverse and the compound Poisson-gamma (Tweedie, 1<p<2) canonical link is μ^(1-p), so log links for gamma and Tweedie are not canonical.

places.quote: | Reciprocal | $1/\mu$ | $1/\eta$ | Gamma (inverse) |
| Tweedie ($1<p<2$) | $\mu^{p}$ | $\mu^{1-p}/(1-p)$ (log in practice) | Pure premium |
| Count | Poisson | Log: $g(\mu) = \ln\mu$ |

requirements.statement: A log link guarantees positive predicted means (exp of the linear predictor), whereas an identity link can predict negative values, so identity links are unsuitable for non-negative responses.

places.quote: The **log link** is standard for insurance severity and frequency models because it guarantees positive fitted values
the identity link lets the linear predictor run below zero, producing impossible negative expected counts
Ordinary least-squares assumes a Normal response, which can produce negative fitted severities and underweights the right skew.

requirements.statement: A normal error structure assigns probability to negative values, so it is unsuitable for modelling a strictly non-negative response.

places.quote: is a symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution on $(-\infty, \infty)$
Ordinary least-squares assumes a Normal response, which can produce negative fitted severities and underweights the right skew.

requirements.statement: Principal component regression replaces the p predictors with the first M principal components (M < p) and fits a regression of the response on those components.

places.quote: It replaces the $p$ predictors $X_1, \dots, X_p$ with the first $M < p$ principal components $Z_1, \dots, Z_M$, then fits a linear model to those components by least squares.

requirements.statement: The first principal component direction is the linear combination of the predictors along which the observations vary the most (has the largest variance).

places.quote: The first component is the direction along which the observations vary the most. Of all combinations with $\sum_j \phi_{j1}^2 = 1$, it has the largest variance.

requirements.statement: Because principal components are driven by variance, predictors should be standardized before computing them, otherwise variables on larger scales dominate the leading components.

places.quote: Standardize each predictor before computing the components. Otherwise the high-variance variables dominate them.

requirements.statement: Each principal component is a linear combination of all original predictors, so PCR does not remove any original feature and is dimension reduction rather than feature selection (unlike the lasso).

places.quote: **Not feature selection.** Every $Z_m$ is a linear combination of all $p$ original predictors, so the fitted model still uses every one of them (see [[Variable Selection]]).

requirements.statement: PCR chooses its components without using the response (unsupervised), so it assumes the directions of greatest predictor variation are the ones associated with the target, which is not guaranteed.

places.quote: **Its assumption.** PCR assumes that the directions in which $X_1, \dots, X_p$ vary most are also the directions associated with $Y$. Nothing guarantees this, because the components are chosen without looking at $Y$.

requirements.statement: Using fewer components than predictors reduces the number of estimated coefficients, trading a small increase in bias for a decrease in variance and thereby reducing overfitting.

places.quote: The fit estimates the $M + 1$ coefficients $\theta_0, \dots, \theta_M$ instead of $p + 1$. The implied $\beta_j$ are forced into the form of the third line, which can bias them. But when $p$ is large relative to $n$, choosing $M \ll p$ can cut their variance a great deal.

requirements.statement: Leave-One-Out Cross Validation (LOOCV) fits the model n times, each time training on all observations but one, and evaluates the fit on the single held-out observation.

places.quote: **$k$-fold**: split the data into $k$ equal parts, fit on $k-1$ and score on the held-out fold, then rotate.
**Leave-one-out (LOOCV):** $\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum \text{MSE}_i$.

requirements.statement: To compute LOOCV error from a table of fitted values by training subset, use only the prediction for the observation omitted from each training subset's fit; fitted values for observations used in training are ignored.

places.quote: **$k$-fold**: split the data into $k$ equal parts, fit on $k-1$ and score on the held-out fold, then rotate.
$\hat{f}$ is fitted on the training data only and scored on the $n_v$ held-out ([[Holdout Sample|hold-out]]) observations.

requirements.statement: The LOOCV mean squared error is CV(n) = (1/n) Σ (y_i − ŷ_(i))², the average of squared errors between each observation and its prediction from the model fit without that observation.

places.quote: **Leave-one-out (LOOCV):** $\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum \text{MSE}_i$.

requirements.statement: When choosing between models by cross-validation, prefer the model with the smaller cross-validated mean squared error.

places.quote: Cross-validation is what turns the [[Bias-Variance Tradeoff]] into a decision: training error falls monotonically with complexity, while CV error is U-shaped, and its minimum marks the right model size
B wins on training error but loses on the hold-out: it is overfitting, so choose A.

requirements.statement: A compound Poisson process S(t) is the sum of N(t) independent, identically distributed random amounts Y_i, where N(t) is a Poisson process counting events (e.g., orders) and is independent of the Y_i.

places.quote: The severities $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ are i.i.d., independent of the counting process $N(t)$
$N$ is the **claim count** (frequency) random variable; $X_i$ are i.i.d. **claim severity** random variables independent of $N$

requirements.statement: For a compound Poisson process with rate λ and i.i.d. amounts Y, Var[S(t)] = λ t E[Y^2], i.e., the variance equals the Poisson mean number of events times the second moment of the amount.

places.quote: \text{Var}(S(t)) = \lambda t\, E[X^2]
When $N \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda)$: $\text{Var}(S) = \lambda \cdot E[X^2]$ (simplification since $\text{Var}(N) = E[N] = \lambda$)

requirements.statement: In a homogeneous Poisson process with rate λ, the number of events in an interval of length t is Poisson with mean λt.

places.quote: N(t) \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda t)
The number of events in any interval of length $t$ has distribution $\text{Poi}(\lambda t)$

requirements.statement: The second moment of a discrete random variable is E[Y^2] = Σ y^2 P(Y = y).

places.quote: E[g(X)] = \sum_i g(x_i)\,P(X = x_i) + \int g(x)\,f(x)\,dx

requirements.statement: Linear splines, local regression, polynomial regression and step functions extend linear regression to capture non-linear relationships between a predictor and the response.

places.quote: A **linear spline** is a line in each region, continuous at each knot.
**Local regression** fits a flexible non-linear function point by point.

requirements.statement: To check a linear regression's fit, plot residuals against the predictor; a random band centered on zero with constant spread indicates the linear form is adequate, while curvature, trends, or jumps indicate non-linearity.

places.quote: | Curved pattern | **Non-linearity** — a transform or polynomial term is needed |

**Mean structure** (right predictors, right form, right [[Link Function|link]]): a [[Residual Plot]] against the fitted values and against each predictor, where curvature means a missing term or transformation;

requirements.statement: Adding model flexibility beyond what the data's true structure requires fits noise, which lowers training error but raises variance and tends to worsen test-set performance (overfitting).

places.quote: Adding terms, interactions, or levels lowers bias and raises variance. Removing them does the reverse.

**Overfitting** is fitting a model so closely to its training data that it follows the noise in that sample as well as the signal, so that it predicts new observations worse than a simpler model would.

requirements.statement: Cook's distance for observation i is D_i = (r_i^2 / p) * h_i/(1 - h_i), where r_i is the standardized (internally studentized) residual, h_i is the leverage, and p is the number of regression parameters.

places.quote: $D_i = \dfrac{e_i^2}{p \cdot \text{MSE}} \cdot \dfrac{h_{ii}}{(1 - h_{ii})^2}$
$$D_i = \frac{r_i^2}{p + 1} \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{1 - h_{ii}}$$

requirements.statement: An observation is classified as influential under Cook's distance when D_i exceeds the chosen threshold (e.g., 1).

places.quote: A common flag is $D_i > 1$; some texts use $4/n$.

requirements.statement: The number of parameters p in a simple linear regression with one predictor and an intercept is 2 (the intercept counts as a parameter).

places.quote: with $p$ the number of coefficients including the intercept
where $p$ is the number of predictors ($p + 1$ coefficients with the intercept)

requirements.statement: Leverage h_i measures how much influence an observation's predictor values have on its own fitted value (the diagonal of the hat matrix); high leverage combined with a large residual yields high influence.

places.quote: A **high-leverage** point is different: its *predictor* values are unusual, measured by the leverage $h_{ii}$ (the $i$-th diagonal of the hat matrix, which depends only on the $x$ values).
Its diagonal entries $h_{ii}$ are the **leverages**: how far each observation's predictor values sit from the rest, and so how hard it can pull the fitted surface toward itself.

requirements.statement: AIC = -2 ln L + 2p, where L is the maximized likelihood and p is the number of estimated parameters.

places.quote: $$\text{AIC} = -2\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) + 2p$$
$\hat{\ell}_M$ is model $M$'s maximized log-likelihood and $p_M$ its number of parameters. $k = 2$ gives [[AIC]]; $k = \ln n$ gives [[BIC]], which penalizes more heavily once $n \geq 8$.

requirements.statement: BIC = -2 ln L + p ln n, where L is the maximized likelihood, p is the number of parameters and n is the number of observations.

places.quote: $$\text{BIC} = -2\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) + p\ln(n)$$
$\hat{\ell}_M$ is model $M$'s maximized log-likelihood and $p_M$ its number of parameters. $k = 2$ gives [[AIC]]; $k = \ln n$ gives [[BIC]], which penalizes more heavily once $n \geq 8$.

requirements.statement: When comparing models by AIC or BIC, the model with the lowest criterion value is preferred, because the criterion penalizes the log-likelihood fit for the number of parameters.

places.quote: **Lower AIC** indicates a better model (better fit relative to complexity)
Lower [[AIC]] or [[BIC]] indicates a better trade-off between fit and complexity

requirements.statement: Deviance is twice the difference between the log-likelihood of the saturated model and the log-likelihood of the fitted model.

places.quote: $$D^* = 2\left[\ell_{\text{sat}} - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\right] = 2\left[\ell(\text{saturated model}) - \ell(\text{fitted model})\right]$$
$$D^* = 2\left[\ell_{\text{saturated}} - \ell_{\text{model}}\right]$$

requirements.statement: The saturated model has a separate free parameter for each observation, so each observation is fitted perfectly (its parameter estimate is set by that observation alone).

places.quote: It compares the fitted model to the **saturated model** (a model with one parameter per observation, achieving perfect fit).
It measures the log-likelihood gap between the model and the saturated model, which has one parameter per record and fits perfectly ($D^* = 0$).

requirements.statement: For an exponential distribution with mean theta, the maximum likelihood estimate of theta is the sample mean (for a single observation, the observation itself).

places.quote: Setting $\ell'(\theta) = -\frac{n}{\theta} + \frac{\sum x_i}{\theta^2} = 0$ gives $\hat{\theta} = \bar{x} = \frac{2+3+5+4+6}{5} = 4$
A sample of $n = 200$ exponential claim sizes has MLE $\hat\theta = \bar{x} = 1{,}500$, and for the exponential $I(\theta) = 1/\theta^2$.

requirements.statement: The exponential log-likelihood for one observation is -ln(theta) - x/theta, and the total log-likelihood for independent observations is the sum of these terms.

places.quote: For $\text{Exp}(\theta)$: $f(x) = \frac{1}{\theta}e^{-x/\theta}$, so $\ell(\theta) = -n\ln\theta - \frac{1}{\theta}\sum x_i$.

requirements.statement: k-fold cross validation splits the data into k folds, repeatedly trains on k-1 folds and validates on the held-out fold, then averages the k validation errors; LOOCV is the special case k = n, holding out one observation each time.

places.quote: **$k$-fold**: split the data into $k$ equal parts, fit on $k-1$ and score on the held-out fold, then rotate.
averages this over $k$ rotating folds, $\text{CV}_{(k)} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_j \text{MSE}_j$; leave-one-out is $k = n$

In $k$-fold [[Cross-Validation|cross-validation]], the data are split into $k$ folds, the model is fitted $k$ times leaving out one fold each time, and $\text{MSE}_j$ is the error on the fold left out (*ISLR*, §5.1.3).

requirements.statement: k-fold cross validation requires only k model fits whereas LOOCV requires n fits, so k-fold with k < n is computationally cheaper, especially for models without a one-fit shortcut such as iteratively fitted GLMs.

places.quote: **Leave-one-out** ($k = n$) is nearly unbiased but has high variance and is expensive — except in a linear model, where the shortcut above gets it from a single fit using the leverages $h_{ii}$
at a cost of only $k$ fits

requirements.statement: Each k-fold training set is smaller than a LOOCV training set (n - 1 observations), so k-fold test error estimates have more upward bias than LOOCV; LOOCV has the advantage in bias reduction.

places.quote: **Leave-one-out** ($k = n$) is nearly unbiased but has high variance and is expensive — except in a linear model, where the shortcut above gets it from a single fit using the leverages $h_{ii}$
It is slightly more biased than LOOCV but less variable, since LOOCV's $n$ fits are nearly identical and their errors highly correlated.

requirements.statement: LOOCV estimates have higher variance than k-fold estimates because the n training sets are nearly identical, making the fitted models and their errors highly correlated; k-fold has an advantage in variance reduction.

places.quote: and the $k$ training sets overlap less than LOOCV's, so the estimate has lower variance
It is slightly more biased than LOOCV but less variable, since LOOCV's $n$ fits are nearly identical and their errors highly correlated.

requirements.statement: The bias of an estimator is its expected value over repeated samples minus the true parameter value: Bias(θ̂) = E[θ̂] − θ.

places.quote: $$\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E[\hat{\theta}] - \theta = 0$$
$$\text{Bias}(\hat\theta) = E[\hat\theta] - \theta$$
$\mathrm{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E[\hat{\theta}] - \theta$

requirements.statement: Bias is a property of the estimator across repeated samples, so the estimates from a single sample cannot by themselves reveal bias; their differences from the true values are just sampling errors.

places.quote: Bias is about the *centre* of the estimator's [[Sampling Distribution]], variance about its *spread* — an estimator can be unbiased and useless (huge variance) or biased and excellent (tiny variance)
its quality is judged by the distribution it has *before* the data are seen. The number it produces from a particular sample is the **estimate**.

requirements.statement: When the regression model is correctly specified (the true relationship is linear in the regressors with independent, mean-zero errors), the OLS estimators of the intercept and slope are unbiased.

places.quote: OLS is the [[Maximum Likelihood Estimation|MLE]] under Normal errors, and by Gauss–Markov it is the [[Minimum Variance|minimum-variance]] linear [[Unbiasedness|unbiased]] estimator whenever the errors have mean zero, are uncorrelated and have constant variance

**Properties**: if the errors have mean zero, OLS is [[Unbiasedness|unbiased]], with $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ and $\hat\sigma^2 = \text{RSS}/(n - p - 1)$.

requirements.statement: Ridge regression chooses coefficients to minimize RSS plus lambda times the sum of squared slope coefficients, while lasso minimizes RSS plus lambda times the sum of absolute values of the slope coefficients.

places.quote: $$\text{Ridge:}\quad \min_{\beta}\ \mathrm{RSS} + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^{2}$$ … $$\text{Lasso:}\quad \min_{\beta}\ \mathrm{RSS} + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert\beta_j\rvert$$

requirements.statement: When the tuning parameter lambda is 0 the penalty vanishes and ridge/lasso give the unconstrained least squares estimates; as lambda approaches infinity the penalty dominates and the slope coefficients shrink toward zero.

places.quote: $\lambda = 0$ returns least squares; $\lambda \to \infty$ drives every coefficient to zero.

requirements.statement: Ridge regression shrinks coefficients toward zero but does not set any exactly to zero, so it retains all predictors, whereas the lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero and therefore performs variable selection, yielding a model with no more variables than ridge.

places.quote: **Ridge** ($\ell_2$) shrinks all coefficients smoothly and keeps every predictor … **Lasso** ($\ell_1$) sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so it performs [[Variable Selection]] as part of the fit
Fit all $p$ predictors with a penalty that sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so the selection happens within the fit

requirements.statement: The tuning parameter lambda is selected by cross-validation: compute the cross-validation error over a grid of lambda values and choose the lambda with the smallest error.

places.quote: Standardize the predictors, fit over a grid of $\lambda$, and pick $\lambda$ by 10-fold CV
$$\hat{\lambda} = \arg\min_{\lambda}\ \text{CV}_{(k)}(\lambda)$$

requirements.statement: Ridge regression in budget (constrained) form chooses the coefficient estimates that minimize the residual sum of squares subject to the sum of squared slope coefficients being at most the budget parameter s.

places.quote: \text{Budget form:}\quad \min_{\beta}\ \mathrm{RSS} \ \text{ subject to } \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^{2} \le s \ \text{(ridge)} \ \text{ or } \sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert\beta_j\rvert \le s \ \text{(lasso)}

requirements.statement: The intercept is not penalized in ridge regression, so the constraint applies only to the slope coefficients (sum of squared slopes ≤ s) and the intercept is chosen freely.

places.quote: The intercept is left unpenalized

requirements.statement: To find a constrained estimate from a grid of candidate parameter values, keep only the candidates satisfying the constraint and select the one with the smallest residual sum of squares.

places.quote: $$\text{Budget form:}\quad \min_{\beta}\ \mathrm{RSS} \ \text{ subject to } \sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^{2} \le s \ \text{(ridge)} \ \text{ or } \sum_{j=1}^{p}\lvert\beta_j\rvert \le s \ \text{(lasso)}$$

requirements.statement: A cubic spline is a piecewise cubic polynomial joined at knots, with the curve and its first and second derivatives continuous at each knot.

places.quote: A **cubic spline** is continuous, with continuous first and second derivatives, so it uses $K + 4$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: A cubic spline with K knots uses K + 4 degrees of freedom (including the intercept): a full cubic in the first region plus one extra cubic-term coefficient per knot.

places.quote: A **cubic spline** is continuous, with continuous first and second derivatives, so it uses $K + 4$ degrees of freedom.
