requirements.statement: The waiting time until the nth event of a Poisson process, being a sum of n independent exponential interarrival times, follows a gamma distribution with shape n and rate lambda.

places.quote: The waiting time $S_n = T_1 + \cdots + T_n$ to the $n$-th event follows a [[Gamma]] distribution with shape $n$ and rate $\lambda$
The arrival time $S_n$ of the $n$-th event is Gamma (Erlang) with shape $n$ and rate $\lambda$, mean $n/\lambda$ and variance $n/\lambda^2$
The sum of $n$ independent $\text{Exp}(\theta)$ variables follows $\text{Gamma}(n, \theta)$

requirements.statement: For a gamma distribution with shape n and rate lambda, the mean is n/lambda and the variance is n/lambda^2.

places.quote: The arrival time $S_n$ of the $n$-th event is Gamma (Erlang) with shape $n$ and rate $\lambda$, mean $n/\lambda$ and variance $n/\lambda^2$
$E[X] = \alpha\theta$, $\text{Var}(X) = \alpha\theta^2$, and coefficient of variation $CV = 1/\sqrt{\alpha}$

requirements.statement: A kernel density estimate at x is the average over the n observations of the kernel function centered at each observation: f~(x) = (1/n) * sum of k_{y_i}(x).

places.quote: Equivalently, the kernel centred at an observation $y$ is $k_y(x) = \frac{1}{b}\,w\!\left(\frac{x - y}{b}\right)$, and $\hat{f}(x)$ is the average of $k_{x_1}(x), \ldots, k_{x_n}(x)$.

requirements.statement: The rectangular (uniform) kernel with bandwidth b centered at y equals 1/(2b) for y - b <= x <= y + b and 0 otherwise.

places.quote: each observation is spread evenly over $[y - b,\ y + b]$ at height $\frac{1}{2b}$, so $\hat{f}(x)$ is the number of observations within $b$ of $x$, divided by $2bn$.

requirements.statement: The triangular kernel with bandwidth b centered at y equals (b - |x - y|)/b^2 for y - b <= x <= y + b and 0 otherwise.

places.quote: a tent of height $\frac{1}{b}$ over $[y - b,\ y + b]$, so $k_y(x) = \frac{b - |x - y|}{b^2}$.

requirements.statement: An observation contributes to a kernel estimate at x only if x lies within the bandwidth of that observation (|x - y| <= b); observations farther away contribute zero, and an observation exactly at distance b contributes zero under the triangular kernel.

places.quote: so $\hat{f}(x)$ is the number of observations within $b$ of $x$, divided by $2bn$.

requirements.statement: A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true; its probability is the significance level, computed as the probability of the critical region under H0.

places.quote: A **Type I Error** occurs when a [[Hypothesis Testing|hypothesis test]] incorrectly **rejects a true null hypothesis** $H_0$.
Rejecting a true $H_0$ is a [[Type I Error]], so $\alpha$ is its probability by construction.

requirements.statement: The sum of n independent Bernoulli(q) random variables is binomial with parameters n and q, with mean nq and variance nq(1-q).

places.quote: The **Binomial Distribution** $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ models the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each with probability of success $p$.
A binomial$(n, p)$ is approximately $N\big(np,\ np(1-p)\big)$ and a Poisson$(\lambda)$ approximately $N(\lambda, \lambda)$ for large $n$ or $\lambda$ — each is a sum of i.i.d. pieces.

requirements.statement: For large n, approximate a binomial probability with a normal distribution having the same mean and variance, standardizing to Z and using the standard normal table.

places.quote: For large $n$, $S_n$ is approximately $N(n\mu,\, n\sigma^2)$ regardless of the original distribution
The recipe: identify $n$, compute $E[S_n] = n\mu$ and $\text{Var}(S_n) = n\sigma^2$ ([[Moments for Linear Combinations]]), standardise, look up $\Phi$.

requirements.statement: When approximating a discrete integer-valued distribution by a normal, apply a continuity correction: P(S ≥ k) is approximated using k − 0.5 as the cutoff.

places.quote: When approximating a **discrete** variable (a [[Binomial Distribution|binomial]] or [[Poisson Distribution|Poisson]] count) by a normal, apply the continuity correction: $P(X \leq k) \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{k + 0.5 - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$
**Continuity correction.** When $S_n$ is integer-valued … widen the event by half a unit first: … $P(S_n \ge k) \approx 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{k - 0.5 - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\right)$

requirements.statement: The significance level of a hypothesis test is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true (the Type I error probability), computed under the null value of the parameter.

places.quote: $$\alpha = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true})$$
$$\alpha = \text{Power}(\theta_0) = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true})$$

requirements.statement: The sum of n independent Bernoulli(q) random variables follows a Binomial(n, q) distribution.

places.quote: The **Binomial Distribution** $X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)$ models the number of successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each with probability of success $p$.

requirements.statement: For S ~ Binomial(n, q), Pr(S = s) = C(n, s) q^s (1-q)^(n-s).

places.quote: $$P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$$

requirements.statement: Raising the critical value k shrinks the rejection region {S ≥ k} and so lowers the significance level, so the smallest valid k is found by accumulating upper-tail probabilities until they exceed the allowed level.

places.quote: $$P\left(T \ge c \mid H_0\right) = \alpha$$
lowering $\alpha$ shrinks the rejection region and so lowers power.

requirements.statement: For independent samples from normal distributions with sample sizes n1 and n2, the ratio (S1²/σ1²)/(S2²/σ2²) follows an F distribution with n1−1 numerator and n2−1 denominator degrees of freedom.

places.quote: | $F = \dfrac{S_1^2/\sigma_1^2}{S_2^2/\sigma_2^2}$ | $F_{n_1-1,\,n_2-1}$ | Two-variance test |

**Two normal variances:** for independent normal samples of sizes $n_X$ and $n_Y$, $\dfrac{S_X^2/\sigma_X^2}{S_Y^2/\sigma_Y^2} \sim F(n_X - 1,\ n_Y - 1)$, using the [[Sample Variance|sample variances]].

requirements.statement: If X follows an F distribution with (a, b) degrees of freedom, then 1/X follows an F distribution with (b, a) degrees of freedom, so the ratio can be inverted by swapping the degrees of freedom.

places.quote: **Reciprocal:** $1/F \sim F(m, n)$. A lower-tail critical value is therefore the reciprocal of an upper-tail one with the degrees of freedom swapped: the value below which $F(n, m)$ falls with probability $\alpha$ is $1/c$, where $c$ is the upper-$\alpha$ point of $F(m, n)$.

The lower point comes from $F_{1-\alpha,\,
u_1,\,
u_2} = 1/F_{\alpha,\,
u_2,\,
u_1}$.

requirements.statement: To test a hypothesis about the ratio of two normal variances, compute the F statistic under H0 (the hypothesized variance relation makes the unknown variances cancel) and compare it with the F distribution.
requirements.concept: Hypothesis Test for Equality of Variances

places.quote: For two variances, $F = S_1^2/S_2^2$ is compared with $F_{\alpha,\,n_1-1,\,n_2-1}$.
Under $H_0$, $s_A^2/s_B^2 \sim F(10, 8)$, and the observed ratio is $2.4/0.8 = 3.0$.

requirements.statement: The p-value is the probability, under H0, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed value in the direction of the alternative hypothesis (an upper-tail probability when large values favor H1).

places.quote: $$\text{p-value} = P(\text{test statistic as extreme or more extreme} \mid H_0 \text{ true})$$
A **p-Value** is the probability, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained.

requirements.statement: Obtain the observed test statistic from a given p-value by finding the corresponding percentile (e.g., the 99th percentile for an upper-tail p-value of 1%) of the F distribution from an F table.

places.quote: Find the denominator row, the upper-tail area, then the numerator column.

Here $z_\alpha$, $t_{\alpha,
u}$, $\chi^2_{\alpha,
u}$ and $F_{\alpha,
u_1,
u_2}$ are *upper* $\alpha$ points — the value with probability $\alpha$ above it.

requirements.statement: An exponential distribution with mean θ has variance θ², so the variance determines the mean (θ equals the square root of the variance).

places.quote: $E[X] = \theta$, $\text{Var}(X) = \theta^2$, and $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/\theta}$

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution with mean θ has CDF F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/θ} for x ≥ 0.

places.quote: $E[X] = \theta$, $\text{Var}(X) = \theta^2$, and $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/\theta}$

requirements.statement: The median of a distribution is the value m satisfying F(m) = 0.5, i.e., the 50th percentile.
The k-th order statistic of a sample is its k-th smallest value, and a trimmed mean averages the sample after discarding the lowest and highest values.

places.quote: Given a sample $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$, the $k$-th order statistic $X_{(k)}$ is the $k$-th smallest value.

requirements.statement: The minimum of m independent exponential random variables with mean mu is exponential with mean mu/m (the rate is the sum of the rates).

places.quote: $P\bigl(X_{(1)} > x\bigr) = \bigl[1 - F_1(x)\bigr]\bigl[1 - F_2(x)\bigr]\cdots\bigl[1 - F_n(x)\bigr]$
an exponential with mean $\theta/k$ has survival $e^{-kx/\theta} = S(x)^k$

requirements.statement: By the memoryless property of the exponential distribution, after the smallest lifetime occurs the remaining lifetimes behave as fresh independent exponentials with the same mean.

places.quote: A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.

requirements.statement: For n iid exponentials with mean mu, the expected k-th order statistic is the sum of the mean gaps mu/n + mu/(n-1) + ... + mu/(n-k+1), since each gap between successive order statistics is exponential with mean mu/(number still surviving).

resolution.quote: So the expected k-th order statistic of n i.i.d. exponentials is the sum of the mean gaps, each gap's mean being the individual mean divided by the number still surviving.
resolution.note: written from Sheffield, MIT OCW 18.440 Lecture 20 slide 15, https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-440-probability-and-random-variables-spring-2014/9c364e256bcc2b34ba6dd73025e8bcb2_MIT18_440S14_Lecture20.pdf, and Wikipedia Order statistic (Rényi representation); checked by 2026-10-30T21:37Z/a2ck

requirements.statement: Expectation is linear, so the expected value of an average of random variables equals the average of their expected values, even when the variables are dependent (as order statistics are).

places.quote: E\!\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i]

requirements.statement: The maximum of n independent identically distributed random variables is at most y only if every one is at most y, so its CDF is the nth power of the individual CDF: F_max(y) = [F(y)]^n.

places.quote: $P\bigl(X_{(n)} \le x\bigr) = F_1(x)\,F_2(x)\cdots F_n(x)$
the maximum has $P(X_{(n)} \le x) = F(x)^n$ and the minimum has $P(X_{(1)} > x) = [1 - F(x)]^n$.

requirements.statement: The Weibull distribution with scale θ and shape τ has CDF F(y) = 1 - exp(-(y/θ)^τ), with density f(y) = τ(y/θ)^τ e^{-(y/θ)^τ} / y.

places.quote: f(x) = \frac{\tau\,(x/\theta)^{\tau}\,e^{-(x/\theta)^{\tau}}}{x}, \quad x > 0 … F(x) = 1 - e^{-(x/\theta)^{\tau}}

requirements.statement: The p-th percentile of a distribution is the value x at which the CDF equals p, so it is found by setting F(x) = p and solving for x.

places.quote: When $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing, it is the value that solves $F(x_p) = p$, found by inverting the CDF.

requirements.statement: The odds of success are π/(1−π), and the log-odds (logit) is ln(π/(1−π)).

places.quote: $\pi/(1-\pi)$ is the **odds**; the model is linear in the log-odds, so $e^{\beta_j}$ is the **odds ratio** for a one-unit increase in $x_j$ — the coefficient's natural interpretation

requirements.statement: A logistic regression model with one predictor specifies ln(π/(1−π)) = b0 + b1·x, so the log-odds is linear in the predictor.

places.quote: $$\ln\!\left(\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p$$

requirements.statement: To recover the coefficients from two fitted probabilities, convert each to log-odds, take the slope as the change in log-odds divided by the change in x, and get the intercept by subtracting slope times x from a log-odds value.

places.quote: $$\ln\!\left(\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p$$
$\pi/(1-\pi)$ is the **odds**; the model is linear in the log-odds, so $e^{\beta_j}$ is the **odds ratio** for a one-unit increase in $x_j$

requirements.statement: Ridge regression chooses the coefficients that minimize the residual sum of squares plus a penalty λ times the sum of squared slope coefficients, RSS + λ Σ_{j=1}^p β_j².

places.quote: $$\text{Ridge:}\quad \min_{\beta}\ \mathrm{RSS} + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^{2}$$

requirements.statement: As the tuning parameter λ increases, ridge coefficient estimates shrink toward zero, and they approach zero as λ → ∞; at λ = 0 they equal the least squares estimates.

places.quote: $\lambda = 0$ returns least squares; $\lambda \to \infty$ drives every coefficient to zero.

requirements.statement: The ridge shrinkage penalty is applied only to the slope coefficients β_1,...,β_p and not to the intercept β_0.

places.quote: The intercept is left unpenalized

requirements.statement: Least squares coefficient estimates are scale equivariant (multiplying a predictor by c scales its coefficient by 1/c), whereas ridge coefficient estimates are not, so predictors should be standardized before fitting ridge regression.

places.quote: Predictors must be **standardized** first: the penalty is not scale-invariant, so a variable measured in thousands would otherwise be penalized differently from one measured in units

requirements.statement: Shrinking coefficients (increasing λ) in ridge regression reduces variance at the cost of increased bias, and test error improves when the variance reduction outweighs the added bias.

places.quote: It trades a little bias for a large reduction in variance
shrinking a volatile class estimate toward the overall mean accepts bias to cut variance, and lowers [[Mean Square Error]]

requirements.statement: In a regression with a binary (0/1) dummy variable, the category coded 0 is the baseline, and the intercept equals the expected response for the baseline category when the other predictors are zero.

places.quote: - A categorical predictor with $k$ levels is represented using $k-1$ **indicator (dummy) variables**; the omitted level is the **reference level**, absorbed into the intercept (see [[Parameter Estimate Tables]])
- The **reference level** of a categorical predictor is absorbed into the intercept; other levels are interpreted relative to it

requirements.statement: The coefficient on a dummy variable is the expected difference in response between that category and the baseline category, holding other predictors fixed.

places.quote: Territory B's expected claim frequency is about **22% higher** than Territory A, and Territory C's is about **10% lower**, holding all else equal.
- The **reference level** of a categorical predictor is absorbed into the intercept; other levels are interpreted relative to it

requirements.statement: Recoding a binary dummy variable (swapping which category is 0 and 1) only changes the baseline; the model spans the same column space, so fitted values are unchanged, the other coefficients stay the same, and the dummy coefficient changes sign.

places.quote: The indicators add up to the constant column, so the fit is unchanged and each level gets its own intercept.

requirements.statement: To find the intercept after changing the baseline category, compute the original model's fitted value for the new baseline group with other predictors at zero (original intercept plus that group's dummy coefficient).

places.quote: the omitted level is the **reference level**, absorbed into the intercept
The **reference level** of a categorical predictor is absorbed into the intercept; other levels are interpreted relative to it

requirements.statement: For a compound Poisson process with rate λ, the variance of aggregate losses is Var(S) = λ·E[Y²], where Y is the individual payment amount (rate times the second moment of the payment).

places.quote: \text{Var}(S(t)) = \lambda t\, E[X^2]
When $N \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda)$: $\text{Var}(S) = \lambda \cdot E[X^2]$ (simplification since $\text{Var}(N) = E[N] = \lambda$)

requirements.statement: With an ordinary deductible d, the payment per loss is Y = (X − d)+, which is zero when the loss X is at most d and X − d otherwise.

places.quote: If the loss $X$ is less than or equal to the deductible $d$, the insurer pays nothing; above $d$ it pays the excess $X - d$

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: given X > d, the excess X − d is exponential with the same mean θ, and Pr(X > d) = e^(−d/θ).

places.quote: A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.

requirements.statement: The second moment of an exponential random variable with mean θ is 2θ².

places.quote: [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] $E[X^n] = n!\,\theta^n$

requirements.statement: Compute the second moment of a per-loss payment under a deductible by conditioning: E[Y²] = Pr(X > d)·E[(X−d)² | X > d].

places.quote: **Thinning** carries over: claims of a given type (e.g. those exceeding a [[Deductible]]) form their own compound Poisson process, with rate $\lambda P(X > d)$ and severity distributed as the conditional excess
The cost per loss is $E[(X - d)_+] = e_X(d)\,S_X(d)$

requirements.statement: R-squared equals 1 minus RSS divided by TSS, i.e., the proportion of total variation in the response explained by the regression.

places.quote: $$R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SS}_\text{Res}}{\text{SS}_\text{Tot}}$$
measures the proportion of total variance in the response variable $Y$ that is explained by the model.

requirements.statement: The total sum of squares (TSS) is the sum of squared deviations of the observed responses from their sample mean, Σ(y_i − ȳ)².

places.quote: $$\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$$

requirements.statement: The residual sum of squares (RSS) is the sum of squared differences between observed and fitted responses, Σ(y_i − ŷ_i)².

places.quote: The **Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)** (also called the **Sum of Squared Errors, SSE**) measures the total unexplained variability in a regression model — the sum of squared differences between observed and fitted values.

requirements.statement: Cook's distance for observation i in a linear regression is D_i = e_i^2/(p·σ^2) · h_ii/(1−h_ii)^2, where e_i is the residual, p the number of regression parameters (columns of X), σ^2 the error variance estimate, and h_ii the leverage.

places.quote: $$D_i = \frac{r_i^2}{p + 1} \cdot \frac{h_{ii}}{1 - h_{ii}}$$
$D_i = \dfrac{e_i^2}{p \cdot \text{MSE}} \cdot \dfrac{h_{ii}}{(1 - h_{ii})^2}$ with $p$ the number of coefficients including the intercept.

requirements.statement: The leverage h_ii of observation i is the i-th diagonal element of the hat matrix H = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ.

places.quote: Its diagonal entries $h_{ii}$ are the **leverages**: how far each observation's predictor values sit from the rest, and so how hard it can pull the fitted surface toward itself.
leverage $h_{ii}$ (the $i$-th diagonal of the hat matrix, which depends only on the $x$ values)

requirements.statement: The residual of observation i is e_i = y_i − ŷ_i, where the fitted values are ŷ = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy = Hy.

places.quote: $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{y}$$
$$e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i$$

requirements.statement: The number of parameters p in Cook's distance equals the number of columns of the design matrix X, including the intercept column of 1s.

places.quote: $D_i = \dfrac{e_i^2}{p \cdot \text{MSE}} \cdot \dfrac{h_{ii}}{(1 - h_{ii})^2}$ with $p$ the number of coefficients including the intercept.

The **design matrix** $\mathbf{X}$ is the $n \times (p+1)$ matrix that holds a regression's predictor values: one row per observation, one column per coefficient, with a leading column of ones for the intercept.

requirements.statement: An observation is classified as influential under Cook's distance when D_i exceeds the threshold (here 1); a high-leverage point with h_ii near 1 can have a large D_i even with a tiny residual.

places.quote: A common flag is $D_i > 1$; some texts use $4/n$.
A high-leverage point can be influential without having a large residual, because it pulls the fit toward itself

requirements.statement: In a linear regression model with an intercept, the intercept is the coefficient on the design-matrix column in which every entry equals 1; a column of 0/1 values is an indicator variable, not the intercept.

places.quote: The **design matrix** $\mathbf{X}$ is the $n \times (p+1)$ matrix that holds a regression's predictor values: one row per observation, one column per coefficient, with a leading column of ones for the intercept.

requirements.statement: The least-squares (OLS) estimator of the coefficient vector is beta-hat = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y, with each entry estimating the coefficient on the corresponding column of X.

places.quote: $$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}$$
$$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$$
$$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}$$

requirements.statement: The (j,j) diagonal entry of X^T X is the sum of squares of column j, so for the all-ones intercept column it equals the number of observations n.
To test whether added terms (e.g., an interaction) are significant, use a nested-model F-test comparing the reduced model to the full model that adds those parameters.

places.quote: When $\phi$ is estimated, use $F = \dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\Delta p\,\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$ on $(\Delta p,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom

When $\phi$ is unknown, estimate it from the full model and use the $F$ form $F = \dfrac{(D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}})/r}{\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$, built from the *unscaled* deviances, on $(r,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom.
to test $k$ added parameters, $\dfrac{D_S - D_B}{k\,\hat{\phi}_B}$ is compared with $F(k,\ n - p_B)$, where $D_S$ and $D_B$ are the unscaled [[Deviance|deviances]] of the small and big models

requirements.statement: The F-statistic is F = [(D_reduced − D_full)/(df_reduced − df_full)] / [D_full/df_full residual], where the numerator degrees of freedom equal the number of added parameters and the denominator uses the full model's residual degrees of freedom.

places.quote: When $\phi$ is estimated, use $F = \dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\Delta p\,\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$ on $(\Delta p,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom
when $\phi$ has to be estimated, comparing nested models that differ by $r$ parameters uses the $F$ statistic $\frac{\Delta D/r}{\hat\phi}$ instead, with $\hat\phi$ from the larger model

When $\phi$ is unknown, estimate it from the full model and use the $F$ form $F = \dfrac{(D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}})/r}{\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$, built from the *unscaled* deviances, on $(r,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: For a Normal response with identity link, the deviance equals the residual sum of squares, and a common scale factor cancels in the F ratio.

places.quote: For a Normal linear model the unscaled deviance is the **residual sum of squares**, $D = \text{RSS} = \sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$, so $D^* = \text{RSS}/\sigma^2$
For a normal linear model the deviances are residual sums of squares and this $F$ is exact

requirements.statement: The improvement in sum of squares (deviance) from adding terms equals the reduced model's deviance minus the full model's deviance, so the full model's deviance is the reduced model's deviance minus the improvement.

places.quote: **Analysis of Deviance**: for nested models, $\dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\phi} \approx \chi^2_{\Delta p}$ when $\phi$ is known (large samples).
For a GLM this statistic is the **difference in deviances divided by the dispersion**, $-2\ln\Lambda = (D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}})/\phi$, with $D$ the unscaled deviance

requirements.statement: The F-statistic is compared with an F distribution with numerator df equal to the number of added parameters and denominator df equal to the full model's residual df; a large F indicates the added terms are significant.

places.quote: When $\phi$ is estimated, use $F = \dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\Delta p\,\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$ on $(\Delta p,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom

When $\phi$ is unknown, estimate it from the full model and use the $F$ form $F = \dfrac{(D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}})/r}{\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$, built from the *unscaled* deviances, on $(r,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom.
to test $k$ added parameters, $\dfrac{D_S - D_B}{k\,\hat{\phi}_B}$ is compared with $F(k,\ n - p_B)$, where $D_S$ and $D_B$ are the unscaled [[Deviance|deviances]] of the small and big models

requirements.statement: In k-fold cross-validation, the data are randomly split into k folds of roughly equal size, and the model is fit k times, each time holding out one fold as the validation set and training on the other k-1 folds.

places.quote: **$k$-fold**: split the data into $k$ equal parts, fit on $k-1$ and score on the held-out fold, then rotate.

In $k$-fold [[Cross-Validation|cross-validation]], the data are split into $k$ folds, the model is fitted $k$ times leaving out one fold each time, and $\text{MSE}_j$ is the error on the fold left out (*ISLR*, §5.1.3).

requirements.statement: In k-fold cross-validation each observation belongs to exactly one fold, so it is in the validation set once and in the training set in the other k-1 fits.

places.quote: **$k$-fold**: split the data into $k$ equal parts, fit on $k-1$ and score on the held-out fold, then rotate.

In $k$-fold [[Cross-Validation|cross-validation]], the data are split into $k$ folds, the model is fitted $k$ times leaving out one fold each time, and $\text{MSE}_j$ is the error on the fold left out (*ISLR*, §5.1.3).

requirements.statement: The bootstrap standard error of an estimator is the standard deviation of the estimates computed from the B bootstrap samples, used to approximate the estimator's sampling variability.

places.quote: The **bootstrap** estimates the sampling variability of a statistic by resampling the observed data *with replacement* $B$ times and looking at the spread of the statistic across the resamples.

requirements.statement: The bootstrap standard error is SE_B = sqrt( (1/(B-1)) * sum over r of (estimate_r - mean of estimates)^2 ), i.e. the sample standard deviation with divisor B-1.

places.quote: $$\mathrm{SE}_B(\hat{\alpha}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_{r=1}^{B}\left(\hat{\alpha}^{*r} - \bar{\hat{\alpha}}^{*}\right)^{2}}$$

requirements.statement: In simple linear regression, the 95% confidence interval for the mean response E(Y) at x0 is ŷ0 ± t(0.025, n-2)·s·sqrt(1/n + (x0 - x̄)²/Sxx).
requirements.concept: Confidence Interval for Mean Response in Linear Regression

requirements.statement: In simple linear regression, the 95% prediction interval for a new observation Y at x0 is ŷ0 ± t(0.025, n-2)·s·sqrt(1 + 1/n + (x0 - x̄)²/Sxx).

places.quote: the interval is $\hat{y}_0 \pm t_{n-p-1}\,s\sqrt{1 + \mathbf{x}_0^{\top}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0}$.

requirements.statement: Confidence and prediction intervals in simple linear regression are both centered on the fitted line and are narrowest at x0 = x̄, widening symmetrically toward the ends of the data range.
requirements.concept: Confidence Interval for Mean Response in Linear Regression

requirements.statement: A prediction interval is always wider than the confidence interval for the mean response because of the extra variance of a new observation, so it encloses most data points (about 95%) and has nearly parallel bands, while the confidence interval is narrow and hugs the fitted line.

places.quote: A prediction interval must also allow for the random shock the new observation will carry, so it is always wider.

requirements.statement: Variable selection means the fitted model leaves some predictors out entirely, i.e. their coefficient estimates are exactly zero.

places.quote: **Variable Selection** is the process of choosing which predictors to include in a model's [[Model Structure]], balancing improved fit against the risk of overfitting and loss of interpretability.
**Lasso** ($\ell_1$) sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so it performs [[Variable Selection]] as part of the fit — good when the truth is sparse

requirements.statement: Lasso regression uses an l1 penalty (lambda times the sum of absolute coefficients), which can set some coefficients exactly to zero when lambda is large enough, so it performs variable selection.

places.quote: **Lasso** ($\ell_1$) sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so it performs [[Variable Selection]] as part of the fit — good when the truth is sparse

| Lasso ([[Regularization]]) | Fit all $p$ predictors with a penalty that sets some coefficients exactly to zero, so the selection happens within the fit; the penalty $\lambda$ is chosen by [[Cross-Validation]] |

requirements.statement: Ridge regression uses an l2 penalty (lambda times the sum of squared coefficients), which shrinks coefficients toward zero but never exactly to zero (for finite lambda), so it keeps all predictors and does not perform variable selection.

places.quote: **Ridge** ($\ell_2$) shrinks all coefficients smoothly and keeps every predictor — good when many predictors each contribute a little.

requirements.statement: Principal components regression and partial least squares are dimension-reduction methods that regress on M new directions, each a linear combination of all p original predictors, so they do not perform variable selection.

places.quote: Every $Z_m$ is a linear combination of all $p$ original predictors, so the fitted model still uses every one of them
As in PCR, the new features are linear combinations of the original predictors, not a subset of them

requirements.statement: A generalized additive model (GAM) replaces each linear term in a regression with a smooth non-linear function of that predictor and sums them: y = beta_0 + sum_j f_j(x_j) + error.

places.quote: A **Generalized Additive Model (GAM)** extends the multiple [[Linear Regression]] model by replacing each linear term $\beta_j x_{ij}$ with a smooth non-linear function $f_j(x_{ij})$, while keeping the model **additive**.

requirements.statement: Each component function of a GAM can be fit using any single-predictor method, such as natural splines, regression splines, smoothing splines, local regression, polynomial regression, or step functions.

places.quote: **Building blocks.** Each $f_j$ can be fit with any of the single-predictor methods: a [[Regression Spline]] (natural splines included), a [[Smoothing Spline]], [[Local Regression]], [[Polynomial Regression]], a [[Step Function]], or a mix.
A smoothing spline can be the building block for one term of a [[Generalized Additive Model]], fit by backfitting.

requirements.statement: A GAM misses interactions between predictors by default because of additivity, but interactions can be added manually as product terms or as low-dimensional interaction functions of two predictors.

places.quote: **The main limitation** is additivity: with many variables, important interactions can be missed. You can add them by hand, either as products $X_j \times X_k$ (see [[Interaction]]) or as low-dimensional interaction functions $f_{jk}(X_j, X_k)$ fit with two-dimensional smoothers.

requirements.statement: The smoothness of a fitted smooth function, such as a smoothing spline, is summarized by its (effective) degrees of freedom.

places.quote: The smoothness of each $f_j$ can be summarized by its degrees of freedom.
so flexibility is measured by $df_\lambda$, the sum of the diagonal of $\mathbf{S}_\lambda$.

requirements.statement: Because a GAM is additive, the effect of each predictor on the response can be examined separately while holding the other predictors fixed, which makes GAMs useful for inference.

places.quote: Because the model is additive, you can examine the effect of each $X_j$ on $Y$ while holding all the other variables fixed.

requirements.statement: Best subset selection fits every possible model of each size and picks the model with the highest R-squared among all models of that size, then compares the best models across sizes using a criterion such as AIC.

places.quote: Fit every combination of the $p$ predictors; keep the best model of each size (lowest RSS, or lowest [[Deviance]] for a GLM), then choose among the sizes as in the last row

requirements.statement: Forward stepwise selection starts from the intercept-only model and at each step adds the single predictor that most improves fit (highest R-squared), keeping all previously added predictors, which yields one nested model per size.

places.quote: Start with no predictors; at each step add the one that most improves the fit; choose among the resulting sizes as in the last row

requirements.statement: Backward stepwise selection starts from the full model and at each step removes the single predictor whose removal leaves the highest R-squared, considering only subsets of the current model, which yields one nested model per size.

places.quote: Start with all predictors (needs $n > p$); at each step remove the least useful one; choose among the sizes as in the last row

requirements.statement: R-squared never decreases as predictors are added, so it can only compare models with the same number of parameters; models of different sizes are compared with a penalized criterion such as AIC, where lower AIC is better.

places.quote: Compare models with different numbers of predictors via [[AIC]] (or $C_p$), [[BIC]], adjusted $R^2$ or [[Cross-Validation]] error — not by raw RSS, $R^2$ or deviance, which always improve as predictors are added
**Lower AIC** indicates a better model (better fit relative to complexity)
$R^2$ **always increases** (or stays the same) when predictors are added, even if they are irrelevant

requirements.statement: Best subset selection searches all models, so its chosen model has AIC no higher than the models chosen by forward or backward stepwise selection; stepwise methods may miss the best model because they are greedy.

places.quote: Best subset selection fits all $2^p$ models … The price is that stepwise selection is not guaranteed to find the best subset: if the best one-predictor model is $\{x_1\}$ but the best two-predictor model is $\{x_2, x_3\}$, forward stepwise cannot reach it, because every later model must keep $x_1$

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: given survival to time s, the remaining lifetime has the same exponential distribution as the original lifetime, so P(T > s + t | T > s) = P(T > t).

places.quote: Its defining property is **memorylessness**: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$, making it the unique continuous distribution with no aging effect

requirements.statement: For an exponential distribution with mean θ, the survival function is S(x) = e^{-x/θ}.

places.quote: Work from the survival function $S(x) = e^{-x/\theta}$ rather than the CDF; almost every exponential question is a tail probability

requirements.statement: The conditional probability of surviving past a later time given survival to an earlier time is P(T > b | T > a) = S(b)/S(a) for b > a.

places.quote: - $_{t}p_x = \dfrac{S(x+t)}{S(x)}$ and $_{t}q_x = 1 - {_t}p_x$
$$P(X \le b \mid X > a) = \frac{P(a < X \le b)}{P(X > a)} = \frac{F(b) - F(a)}{1 - F(a)}, \quad a < b$$

requirements.statement: A piecewise polynomial regression with knots divides the predictor range into regions and fits a separate polynomial in each region, with no continuity constraints at the knots.

places.quote: Placing $K$ knots in the range of $X$ means fitting $K + 1$ polynomials. With no constraints they need not meet, and a piecewise cubic with one knot uses $4 + 4 = 8$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: An unconstrained piecewise polynomial fit can be discontinuous (jump) at the knots, whereas splines are constrained to join at the knots.

places.quote: Placing $K$ knots in the range of $X$ means fitting $K + 1$ polynomials. With no constraints they need not meet, and a piecewise cubic with one knot uses $4 + 4 = 8$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: A cubic spline is a piecewise cubic polynomial constrained to be continuous with continuous first and second derivatives at each knot.

places.quote: A **cubic spline** is continuous, with continuous first and second derivatives, so it uses $K + 4$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: A natural cubic spline is a cubic spline constrained to be linear in the boundary regions beyond the outer knots; it remains continuous.

places.quote: A natural spline adds boundary constraints: the function must be linear below the smallest knot and above the largest.

requirements.statement: A smoothing spline is a natural cubic spline with a knot at every observed predictor value, with smoothness controlled by a penalty, so its fitted curve is continuous.

places.quote: The minimizer is a natural cubic spline with a knot at every unique value of $x_1, \dots, x_n$.

requirements.statement: The number of parameters of a piecewise polynomial of degree d with K knots is (K+1)(d+1), because each of the K+1 regions has its own polynomial with d+1 coefficients.

places.quote: The degree-$d$ row applies the same count to any degree: $d + 1$ coefficients in each of the $K + 1$ regions, minus $d$ continuity constraints at each knot.

requirements.statement: A model with more parameters (higher degrees of freedom) is more flexible and more likely to overfit the data.

places.quote: Adding terms, interactions, or levels lowers bias and raises variance.

Test MSE is U-shaped instead: past the minimum, each added parameter fits errors $\varepsilon_i$ that belong to this sample only and will not recur, so the variance of $\hat{f}$ rises by more than its squared bias falls.

requirements.statement: The survival function equals the exponential of minus the cumulative hazard: S(x) = exp(-H(x)), where H(x) is the integral of the hazard rate function h(t) from the lower support bound to x.

places.quote: $$S(t) = \exp\!\left(-\int_0^t \mu(s)\,ds\right)$$
$$S(t) = \exp\!\left(-\int_0^t \mu(s)\,ds\right)$$

requirements.statement: The survival function is S(x) = 1 - F(x), the complement of the cumulative distribution function.
When the hazard rate is zero below a threshold, no probability mass lies there, so the cumulative hazard starts accumulating at the threshold and S(x)=1 below it.

resolution.note: adds no rule beyond the cumulative-hazard relation S = exp(-integral of the hazard) on Hazard Rate: the integral of a zero hazard is zero, so S = 1 below the threshold and the integral starts there.

requirements.statement: The amount an insurer pays per loss with an ordinary per-loss deductible d is the random variable Y = (X - d)+ = max(X - d, 0), which equals zero when the loss is below the deductible (a per-loss variable, as opposed to a per-payment variable that conditions on X > d).

places.quote: If the loss $X$ is less than or equal to the deductible $d$, the insurer pays nothing; above $d$ it pays the excess $X - d$
$Y^L$ is the payment per loss, which is 0 whenever $X \le d$.

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: given X > d, the excess X - d is exponential with the same mean as X, so the per-payment amount has the same distribution as the original loss.

places.quote: A direct consequence: given $X > d$, the excess $X - d$ is again $\text{Exp}(\theta)$.

requirements.statement: For an exponential distribution with mean theta, the survival function is Pr(X > d) = exp(-d/theta), and the first and second moments are E[X] = theta and E[X^2] = 2 theta^2.

places.quote: - $E[X] = \theta$, $\text{Var}(X) = \theta^2$, and $F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/\theta}$

requirements.statement: Compute moments of a per-loss variable by conditioning on whether the loss exceeds the deductible: E[Y^k] = Pr(X > d) times the k-th moment of the per-payment amount (zero otherwise).

places.quote: The two differ by the factor $P(X > 300) = e^{-0.6} \approx 0.5488$, since $274.4 = 0.5488 \times 500$.
The cost per loss is $E[(X - d)_+] = e_X(d)\,S_X(d)$, which is the [[Payment Random Variable|per-loss]] counterpart of this per-payment quantity.

requirements.statement: The variance of a random variable equals Var(Y) = E[Y^2] - (E[Y])^2, and the standard deviation is its square root.

places.quote: - Efficient computation formula: $\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - \mu^2$ where $\mu = E[X]$
The **standard deviation** ($\sigma$) is the positive square root of the [[Variance]], measuring the spread of a [[Random Variable]] in the same units as the variable itself.

requirements.statement: A parallel system works if at least one component works, so it fails only when every component fails.

places.quote: **Parallel** (works if any works): $\phi = 1 - \prod(1 - x_i)$ and $r = 1 - \prod(1 - p_i)$.

requirements.statement: For a parallel system of independent components with reliabilities r_i, system reliability is 1 minus the product of (1 - r_i).

places.quote: **Parallel** (works if any works): $\phi = 1 - \prod(1 - x_i)$ and $r = 1 - \prod(1 - p_i)$.

requirements.statement: To reach a target parallel-system reliability with the fewest components, use the most reliable components first, since each added component multiplies the failure probability by (1 - r) and a smaller factor reduces it more.

resolution.note: step of this one solution's plan: choosing the most reliable components first to minimise their number; the rule used is the parallel reliability 1 − ∏(1 − r_i) on System Reliability.

requirements.statement: A discrete-time Markov chain is a process whose next-state distribution depends only on the current state, described by a transition probability matrix whose rows sum to 1.

places.quote: A **Markov Chain** is a [[Stochastic Processes|stochastic process]] $\{X_n\}$ on a discrete state space that has the **Markov property**: the next state depends on the past only through the current state. It is governed by a one-step **transition probability matrix** $P$.
$$\sum_{j} P_{ij} = 1 \quad \text{for every row } i$$

requirements.statement: The n-step transition probabilities are the entries of the n-th power of the one-step transition matrix (Chapman-Kolmogorov equations), so the distribution n steps from a given starting state is the corresponding row of P^n.

places.quote: - The $n$-step transition probabilities are the entries of the matrix power $P^n$:

requirements.statement: Build the transition matrix from conditional statements by taking the stated probability for the given transition and its complement for the other transition from the same state.

places.quote: $$\sum_{j} P_{ij} = 1 \quad \text{for every row } i$$
$P_{ij} \geq 0$ is the probability of moving from state $i$ to state $j$ in one step; each row sums to 1

requirements.statement: The expected value of a discrete random variable is the sum of each value times its probability; here the expected number of games is computed using the n-step state distribution.

places.quote: $$E[X] = \begin{cases} \displaystyle\sum_{k} k\, f(k) & \text{(discrete)} \\[6pt] \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\, f(x)\, dx & \text{(continuous)} \end{cases}$$

requirements.statement: When each of N games is won independently with probability p, the expected number of wins is p times the expected number of games (linearity of expectation).

resolution.quote: E[S] = E[N] \cdot E[X]
resolution.note: passage on Aggregate Loss Model (MAS-I syllabus): E[S] = E[N] E[X], here with Bernoulli(p) win indicators as the X_i, so expected wins = p E[games]; the check's miss.

requirements.statement: The stationary (long-run) distribution of a Markov chain is a probability vector π satisfying π = πP, i.e., each state's probability equals the sum of the probabilities of the other states times their transition probabilities into it (balance equations), with probabilities summing to 1.
requirements.concept: Stationary Distribution of a Markov Chain

places.quote: A **stationary distribution** $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{\pi}P = \boldsymbol{\pi}$ with $\sum_i \pi_i = 1$
$$\pi_j = \sum_i \pi_i\, P_{ij} \quad \text{for every } j$$

requirements.statement: A finite, irreducible Markov chain has a unique stationary distribution, and if it is also aperiodic, the long-run probabilities converge to it regardless of the starting state.
requirements.concept: Limiting Distribution of a Markov Chain

places.quote: A finite irreducible chain always has a unique stationary distribution.
Positive recurrent, aperiodic states are called **ergodic** — the setting in which the [[Stationary Distribution]] is also the limit of $P^n_{ij}$.

requirements.statement: A state with a positive self-transition probability (P_{i,i} > 0) has period 1, so an irreducible chain containing such a state is aperiodic.

places.quote: A state with period 1 is **aperiodic**; any state with $P_{ii} > 0$ is aperiodic.

requirements.statement: When states of a chain are interchangeable by symmetry, one can assume they share a common long-run probability, reduce the balance equations to a few unknowns, and verify that the resulting solution satisfies all balance equations, which makes it the unique stationary distribution.
requirements.concept: Stationary Distribution of a Markov Chain

places.quote: A doubly stochastic matrix has a uniform $\boldsymbol{\pi}$.
For a chain with finitely many states the uniform distribution is then stationary, and it is the chain's unique [[Stationary Distribution|stationary distribution]] when the chain is irreducible.
Each column also sums to 1, so the uniform distribution is stationary: $\pi_S = \pi_F = \pi_H = \tfrac13$.

requirements.statement: The waiting time until the n-th event of a Poisson process with rate λ is the sum of n independent exponential interarrival times and therefore follows a gamma distribution with shape n and scale 1/λ.

places.quote: The waiting time $S_n = T_1 + \cdots + T_n$ to the $n$-th event follows a [[Gamma]] distribution with shape $n$ and rate $\lambda$
The sum of $n$ independent $\text{Exp}(\theta)$ variables follows $\text{Gamma}(n, \theta)$
The arrival time $S_n$ of the $n$-th event is Gamma (Erlang) with shape $n$ and rate $\lambda$, mean $n/\lambda$ and variance $n/\lambda^2$

requirements.statement: Interarrival times of a Poisson process with rate λ are independent exponential random variables with mean 1/λ.

places.quote: Interarrival times $T_1, T_2, \ldots$ are i.i.d. $\text{Exponential}(\lambda)$ with mean $1/\lambda$
For a [[Poisson Process]] with rate $\lambda$, the interarrival times are independent and identically distributed [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] variables with mean $1/\lambda$

requirements.statement: Thinning a Poisson process, where each event is independently kept with probability p, gives a Poisson process with rate pλ, so counts over an interval of length t are Poisson with mean pλt.

places.quote: A Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ **thinned** by probability $p$ produces a Poisson process with rate $\lambda p$
$N_1(t) \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda p\, t)$

requirements.statement: A Poisson count whose mean is random with a gamma distribution has an unconditional negative binomial distribution (gamma-Poisson mixture), with variance exceeding the mean.

places.quote: With a [[Gamma]] mixing distribution the unconditional counts are exactly **[[Negative Binomial Distribution|negative binomial]]**

If $\Lambda \sim$ [[Gamma]]$(\alpha, \theta)$ (shape $\alpha$, scale $\theta$), then $N(t)$ is [[Negative Binomial Distribution|negative binomial]] in its failures-count form with $r = \alpha$ and $p = 1/(1 + \theta t)$:

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: the remaining waiting time given that time has already elapsed without an event has the same exponential distribution as the original.

places.quote: Its defining property is **memorylessness**: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$, making it the unique continuous distribution with no aging effect
**Memoryless**: $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$. Time already spent waiting tells you nothing about the wait remaining, so there is no "due for a claim" effect

requirements.statement: Given that exactly n events of a Poisson process occurred in an interval, the event times are distributed as order statistics of n independent uniform random variables on that interval; for n = 1 the single arrival time is uniform on the interval.

places.quote: Given $N(t) = n$, the $n$ arrival times are distributed as the [[Order Statistics]] of $n$ independent $\text{Uniform}(0, t)$ draws — arrivals are "scattered at random" over the interval

requirements.statement: For a Poisson process with a constant rate per unit of exposure, the claim count over E units of exposure is Poisson with mean equal to the rate times E, and its variance equals its mean.

places.quote: The number of events in any interval of length $t$ has distribution $\text{Poi}(\lambda t)$
A defining property is $E[X] = \text{Var}(X) = \lambda$ — the mean and variance are equal

requirements.statement: Claim frequency is the number of claims divided by the exposure (e.g., vehicle-years).

places.quote: **Frequency** is the number of claims per unit of exposure — how often losses happen, as distinct from [[Severity|how much they cost]].
$f$ is the expected number of losses a year from one exposure, its [[Frequency|frequency]]

requirements.statement: For a constant c, E[cX] = c·E[X] and Var(cX) = c²·Var(X), so dividing a random variable by E divides its variance by E².

places.quote: $$\text{Var}(L) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2\,\text{Var}(X_i) + 2\sum_{i < j} c_i c_j\,\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$$

requirements.statement: For Poisson claims, the mean of observed frequency equals the rate regardless of exposure, while its variance equals the rate divided by exposure, so more exposure lowers the variance of observed frequency.

places.quote: $$E[N(t)] = \text{Var}(N(t)) = \lambda t$$
For $n$ i.i.d. variables with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, $\bar{X}$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$

requirements.statement: Exposure is measured in vehicle-years (the number of vehicles times the fraction of the year each is in force), and a claim frequency is expressed per unit of exposure.

places.quote: **Frequency** is the number of claims per unit of exposure — how often losses happen, as distinct from [[Severity|how much they cost]].
A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.

requirements.statement: Expected claim count equals the claim frequency per exposure unit times the total exposure earned, with exposure summed across periods with different fleet sizes weighted by period length.

places.quote: The number of events in any interval of length $t$ has distribution $\text{Poi}(\lambda t)$
Counts over an interval are still Poisson, but the mean is the **integrated** rate over that interval.

requirements.statement: The sum (superposition) of independent Poisson processes is a Poisson process whose rate is the sum of the individual rates, so the total count over a period is Poisson with the summed mean.

places.quote: **Superposition**: two independent Poisson processes with rates $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ combine into a Poisson process with rate $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$

**Poisson Superposition** is the result that the sum of independent [[Poisson Process|Poisson processes]] is itself a Poisson process whose rate is the sum of the individual rates — merging independent claim streams produces one Poisson stream.

requirements.statement: For N ~ Poisson(λ), P(N = k) = e^{-λ} λ^k / k!.

places.quote: $$P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$$
$$P(N(t) = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!}$$

requirements.statement: The limited expected value E[X ∧ u] is the expected value of the loss capped at the limit u, i.e. E[min(X, u)].

places.quote: The **Limited Expected Value** (LEV) of a random variable $X$ at limit $u$ is the expected value of the payment under a policy that pays $X$ up to a maximum of $u$.
$E[X \wedge L]$ is the **limited expected value**, the expected loss capped at $L$.

requirements.statement: For a non-negative loss X, E[X ∧ u] = ∫_0^u Pr(X > x) dx = ∫_0^u S(x) dx.

places.quote: $$E[X \wedge u] = \int_0^u [1 - F(x)]\,dx \quad \text{(for non-negative } X\text{)}$$
$$E[X \wedge u] = \int_0^u S(x)\,dx$$
Since $\text{LAS}(k) = \int_0^k S(x)\,dx$ (Palmer)

requirements.statement: Expectation preserves inequalities: if one random variable is no greater than another for every outcome, its expected value is no greater either.

resolution.quote: Expectation preserves inequalities, so a random variable that never exceeds a constant $c$ has a mean of at most $c$
resolution.note: written from Siegrist, 4.1 Definitions and Basic Properties, increasing and positive properties, https://www.randomservices.org/random/expect/Properties.html; checked by g8-masi-check-A1-2026-10-30

requirements.statement: A survival function is non-increasing, so S(x) ≤ S(u) for x ≥ u, which bounds the extra expected loss from raising a limit from u to u+h by h·S(u).

places.quote: each additional dollar of limit at $x$ adds $S(x)$ — the probability a loss exceeds $x$ — which cannot rise as $x$ rises.
$S(0) = 1$, $S(\infty) = 0$, and $S(t)$ is non-increasing

requirements.statement: Under uniform inflation by factor (1+r), a limited expected value with a fixed limit satisfies E[(kX) ∧ u] = k·E[X ∧ u/k], so it grows by less than the inflation rate when the limit is not indexed.
requirements.concept: Effect of Inflation on Limited Expected Value

places.quote: $$E\big[(1+r)X \wedge u\big] = (1+r)\,E\!\left[X \wedge \tfrac{u}{1+r}\right]$$
a fixed limit **damps** it, raising the capped payment by less than $r$.

requirements.statement: The Pareto limited expected value is E[X ∧ u] = θ/(α−1)·[1 − (θ/(θ+u))^(α−1)] for α ≠ 1, and it gives the expected loss capped at u.

places.quote: | Pareto$(\alpha, \theta)$, $\alpha \neq 1$ | $\dfrac{\theta}{\alpha-1}\!\left[1 - \left(\dfrac{\theta}{\theta+u}\right)^{\alpha-1}\right]$ |
$$E[X \wedge x] = \frac{\theta}{\alpha - 1}\left[1 - \left(\frac{\theta}{x + \theta}\right)^{\alpha - 1}\right]$$

requirements.statement: With an ordinary deductible d and maximum covered loss u, the expected payment per loss is E[X ∧ u] − E[X ∧ d].

places.quote: $$Y^L = (X \wedge u) - (X \wedge d)$$
$$E[Y^L] = \alpha\big(E[X \wedge u] - E[X \wedge d]\big)$$

requirements.statement: Multiplying a Pareto random variable by a constant (e.g. inflation factor 1+r) multiplies θ by that constant and leaves α unchanged, since Pareto is a scale family.

places.quote: A **scale parameter** $\theta$ sets the units: multiplying the loss by a positive constant $c$ multiplies $\theta$ by $c$ and leaves every other parameter unchanged.

resolution.quote: In the exam tables, $\theta$ is the scale parameter of the exponential, gamma, Weibull and Pareto families
resolution.note: retagged Scale and Shape Parameters; the question inflates a Pareto severity; Scale and Shape Parameters defines a scale parameter as one the multiplication multiplies while changing no other, names θ as the Pareto's, and says inflation is handled by changing θ alone.

requirements.statement: To find the effect of inflation on a policy with a fixed deductible and fixed maximum covered loss, inflate the loss distribution, then recompute the limited expected values at the unchanged deductible and limit; the layer is not inflated.

places.quote: If losses grow to $(1+r)X$ and the limit stays fixed, the expected payment is $(1+r)$ times the limited expected value at the deflated limit $u/(1+r)$.
If losses grow to $(1+r)X$ while $d$ and $u$ stay fixed, deflate the limits instead of inflating the losses

requirements.statement: For a compound Poisson aggregate S with Poisson rate λ and individual payment X, Var(S) = λ·E[X²], the second moment of the payment, not λ·Var(X).

places.quote: With $N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, $E[N] = \text{Var}(N) = \lambda$, so the two terms combine into the second moment of a claim: for a compound Poisson $S$, $\text{Var}(S) = \lambda\,E[X^2]$.

The variance uses the **second moment** $E[X^2]$, not the variance of $X$ — this falls out of the compound-variance formula $\text{Var}(S) = E[N]\text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(N)E[X]^2$ with $E[N] = \text{Var}(N) = \lambda t$
When $N \sim \text{Poi}(\lambda)$: $\text{Var}(S) = \lambda \cdot E[X^2]$ (simplification since $\text{Var}(N) = E[N] = \lambda$)

requirements.statement: Thinning a Poisson process, where each event is independently kept with probability p, gives a Poisson process with rate λp that is independent of the process of removed events.

places.quote: **Poisson Thinning** (splitting) is the result that if each event of a [[Poisson Process]] with rate $\lambda$ is independently classified as type 1 with probability $p$ and type 2 with probability $1-p$, the two type counts are themselves **independent** Poisson processes with rates $\lambda p$ and $\lambda(1-p)$.

requirements.statement: For an exponential random variable with mean θ, the second moment is E[X²] = 2θ² (variance θ²).

requirements.statement: A discrete random variable takes only countably many values, while a continuous random variable has a density and assigns probability 0 to every single point.

places.quote: $X$ is **discrete** if its possible values form a finite or countably infinite set, and **continuous** if its probabilities come from a density, $P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ — so its CDF has no jumps and every single value has probability 0.

A **Discrete Random Variable** $X$ is a [[Random Variable]] whose possible values form a finite or countably infinite set — typically a count, such as the number of claims — so its distribution is given by a [[Probability Mass Function (PMF)|probability mass function]] $p(x) = P(X = x)$.

A **Continuous Random Variable** $X$ is a [[Random Variable]] whose [[Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)|CDF]] $F(x)$ is the integral of a [[Probability Density Function (PDF)|density]] $f(x)$, so that probability is area under $f$ and every single value has probability zero.

requirements.statement: A mixed random variable has a distribution with point masses (CDF jumps) combined with a continuous part, so it is neither purely discrete nor purely continuous.

places.quote: A payment under a [[Deductible]], $Y = (X - d)_+$ with $X$ continuous, takes a continuum of values yet puts probability $P(X \le d) > 0$ on the single value 0: it is a **mixed** random variable, neither discrete nor continuous

Insurance payments are often **mixed**. A continuous loss passed through a [[Deductible]] or a [[Benefit Limit|limit]] produces a [[Payment Random Variable|payment]] with a point mass at 0 or at the limit, which is neither purely discrete nor purely continuous.

requirements.statement: With an ordinary deductible d, the payment per loss is (X - d)_+, equal to 0 when X ≤ d and X - d when X > d; the payment per payment is X - d conditional on X > d.

places.quote: If the loss $X$ is less than or equal to the deductible $d$, the insurer pays nothing; above $d$ it pays the excess $X - d$
The payment per payment $Y^P$ is conditional on $X > d$, and $E[Y^L] = P(X > d)\,E[Y^P]$.

requirements.statement: The payment per loss under a deductible has a point mass at 0 equal to P(X ≤ d), so it is a mixed random variable.

places.quote: It has a point mass at zero, $P(Y = 0) = P(X \leq d) = F_X(d)$, so it has a [[Mixture Distribution|mixed distribution]] when $X$ is continuous.
A single value carries probability $0.2$, so **$Y$ is not continuous**. It is mixed: a mass of $0.2$ at zero plus a density of $\tfrac{1}{1{,}000}$ on $(0, 800)$.

requirements.statement: The exponential distribution is memoryless: given X > d, X - d is again exponential with the same mean.

places.quote: Its defining property is **memorylessness**: $P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)$, making it the unique continuous distribution with no aging effect
The exponential is memoryless, so the part of a loss above the deductible has the same mean as the loss itself.

requirements.statement: The exponential CDF is F(x) = 1 - e^{-x/θ}, so P(X ≤ d) = 1 - e^{-d/θ}.

requirements.statement: A mixed random variable has both discrete point masses and a continuous part; its CDF jumps at the point masses and is continuous (rising) elsewhere.

places.quote: The two classes do not cover every case. A payment under a [[Deductible]], $Y = (X - d)_+$ with $X$ continuous, takes a continuum of values yet puts probability $P(X \le d) > 0$ on the single value 0: it is a **mixed** random variable, neither discrete nor continuous

**Mixed (discrete–continuous) type.** A mixture of a point mass and a continuous distribution gives a CDF with a jump, such as an annual loss that is $0$ with positive probability and continuous otherwise.

requirements.statement: A point mass at a value equals the size of the CDF's jump there: P(Y=a) = F(a) - F(a^-); a jump at 0 gives F(0) as the mass at 0, and a mass at an upper limit equals 1 - F(limit^-).

places.quote: A jump in the CDF at $x$ — $F(x)$ greater than its left-hand limit $F(x^-) = P(X < x)$ — is a point mass: the single value $x$ has probability equal to the size of the jump.
It has a point mass at zero, $P(Y = 0) = P(X \leq d) = F_X(d)$

requirements.statement: On a continuous part of the CDF, the density is the derivative of the CDF, f(y) = F'(y).
For a mixed random variable, E[Y] = sum of (value × point mass) over the discrete points plus the integral of y f(y) over the continuous part.

places.quote: $$E[g(X)] = \sum_i g(x_i)\,P(X = x_i) + \int g(x)\,f(x)\,dx$$
Its moments combine a sum over the mass points with an integral over the continuous part.

requirements.statement: For a nonnegative random variable, E[Y] = integral from 0 to infinity of the survival function S(y) = 1 - F(y).

places.quote: For $X \ge 0$ the survival shortcut $E[X] = \int_0^\infty [1 - F(x)]\,dx$ often avoids integration by parts.
$$\mathring{e}_x = E[T_x] = \int_0^{\infty} {}_tp_x\,dt$$

requirements.statement: A mixture distribution arises by first selecting a component at random with given probabilities and then drawing from that component; its density, CDF and survival function are the probability-weighted averages of the components' densities, CDFs and survival functions.

places.quote: Its density (and its [[Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)|CDF]]) is the weighted average of the component densities, with the weights given by a [[Mixing Distribution|mixing distribution]]

**A mixture of exponentials is not exponential.** When $X$ is $\text{Exp}(\theta_1)$ with probability $w$ and $\text{Exp}(\theta_2)$ otherwise (a [[Mixture Distribution|mixture]]), compute a probability within each component and weight by the mixing probabilities

requirements.statement: The survival function of an exponential random variable with mean θ is P(X > x) = e^{-x/θ}.

places.quote: Work from the survival function $S(x) = e^{-x/\theta}$ rather than the CDF; almost every exponential question is a tail probability

requirements.statement: Raw moments of a mixture are the probability-weighted averages of the components' raw moments, so the variance of a mixture is found from the mixed first and second moments (Var = E[X^2] − E[X]^2), not by averaging component variances.

places.quote: The **variance is not linear**: compute $E[X^2] - (E[X])^2$ from the mixed moments, or use the law of total variance ([[Variance for Conditional and Marginal Distributions]]):

requirements.statement: The second raw moment of an exponential random variable with mean θ is 2θ^2 (variance θ^2).

places.quote: Closed forms worth memorising: [[Exponential Distribution|exponential]] $E[X^n] = n!\,\theta^n$

requirements.statement: Law of total variance: Var(X) = E[Var(X|Y)] + Var(E[X|Y]); the mixture variance equals the average component variance plus the variance of the component means.

places.quote: \text{Var}(X) = E\big[\text{Var}(X \mid \Theta)\big] + \text{Var}\big(E[X \mid \Theta]\big)

places.page: Variance for Conditional and Marginal Distributions
places.quote: \text{Var}(X) = E\bigl[\text{Var}(X \mid Y)\bigr] + \text{Var}\bigl(E[X \mid Y]\bigr)

requirements.statement: A weighted sum of independent random variables is not a mixture of their distributions; its variance is the sum of squared-coefficient-weighted variances (Var(aX1 + bX2) = a²Var(X1) + b²Var(X2)), and it generally has a different distribution from the mixture.
requirements.concept: Variance of Sums of Independent Random Variables

places.quote: Coefficients enter the variance **squared**, so $\text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)$ for independent $X, Y$
**Mixing is not adding:** A mixture averages densities. The distribution of the sum of two claims is a [[Convolution|convolution]], which is a different object with a different variance.

requirements.statement: A mixture of a point mass at zero and a continuous distribution has a CDF equal to the weighted sum of the component CDFs, with a jump at zero equal to the zero-loss probability.

places.quote: A mixture of a point mass and a continuous distribution gives a CDF with a jump, such as an annual loss that is $0$ with positive probability and continuous otherwise.
A jump in the CDF at $x$ — $F(x)$ greater than its left-hand limit $F(x^-) = P(X < x)$ — is a point mass: the single value $x$ has probability equal to the size of the jump.

requirements.statement: The p-th percentile of a random variable is the value x at which the CDF equals p, i.e. F(x) = p (the smallest x with F(x) ≥ p).

places.quote: The **Percentile** (or quantile) $x_p$ of a [[Random Variable]] $X$ is the smallest value at which the [[Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)|CDF]] reaches $p$, so at least a proportion $p$ of the distribution lies at or below it.

For a [[Discrete Random Variable|discrete]] $X$ the CDF usually jumps past 0.5 rather than landing on it, so $F(m) = 0.5$ has no solution; the median is then the smallest $m$ with $F(m) \ge 0.5$ — the same rule as for every other [[Percentile]].

requirements.statement: A two-parameter Pareto with shape α and scale θ has survival function S(x) = (θ/(x+θ))^α and CDF F(x) = 1 − (θ/(x+θ))^α for x ≥ 0.

places.quote: $$F(x) = 1 - \left(\frac{\theta}{x + \theta}\right)^{\alpha}$$

requirements.statement: When the target percentile exceeds the probability mass at zero, it lies in the continuous part of the distribution, so the equation F(x)=p is solved using only the continuous component of the mixture.
