places.quote: **Simple regression**: $\hat\beta_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1\bar{x}$, where $S_{xy} = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})$ and $S_{xx} = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2$
$$\hat\beta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2}$$

requirements.statement: A quantile (e.g. quintile) plot for a GLM holdout test sorts holdout policies by predicted value, groups them into equal-exposure bins, and compares average predicted to average actual losses in each bin.
requirements.concept: Model Validation with Holdout Data (Quantile Plots)

places.quote: A **quantile plot** (or lift chart by predicted quantile) sorts a held-out dataset by predicted loss cost, splits it into equal-exposure buckets, and plots the actual against the predicted average in each.

A [[Quantile Plot|quantile plot]] sorts records by predicted loss cost into equal-exposure buckets and compares actual with predicted in each, judged on accuracy, monotonicity and the spread between the first and last buckets.

requirements.statement: The actual-to-predicted ratio for a group is total actual losses divided by total predicted losses; a ratio near 1 indicates good fit.
requirements.concept: Model Validation with Holdout Data (Quantile Plots)

places.quote: Overall the ratio is $\$4{,}048{,}000 / \$4{,}000{,}000 = 1.012$, so the model is well balanced in total.
Reading A/E the wrong way up: $\text{A/E} > 1$ means actual exceeded expected, so for claims the model is light.

requirements.statement: Model fit in a group is judged by how far its actual-to-predicted ratio deviates from 1 (relative error), not by the dollar size of the gap between actual and predicted.
requirements.concept: Model Validation with Holdout Data (Quantile Plots)

places.quote: The **12+ band is under-predicted by 15%**, a sign that the fitted vehicle-age curve has the wrong shape at the old end
$\text{Error}_q$ is each approach's percent error in quantile $q$.

requirements.statement: To run a quantile (decile/quintile) plot on a holdout sample, sort the holdout records by the model's predicted value, split them into equal-count groups, and compare the average predicted to the average actual value in each group.

places.quote: A **quantile plot** (or lift chart by predicted quantile) sorts a held-out dataset by predicted loss cost, splits it into equal-exposure buckets, and plots the actual against the predicted average in each.

A [[Quantile Plot|quantile plot]] sorts records by predicted loss cost into equal-exposure buckets and compares actual with predicted in each, judged on accuracy, monotonicity and the spread between the first and last buckets.

requirements.statement: A better model has actual-to-predicted ratios close to 1 in every quantile, not just overall, because an overall ratio near 1 only shows total predicted equals total actual and can hide offsetting errors at the ends.

places.quote: The **12+ band is under-predicted by 15%**, a sign that the fitted vehicle-age curve has the wrong shape at the old end, for example a linear term forcing a trend the data don't follow there.
$\text{Error}_q$ is each approach's percent error in quantile $q$. The winner has the flatter error line, centred on zero.

requirements.statement: A better model separates risks more: the actual results of its highest-predicted group differ more from those of its lowest-predicted group (a wider actual spread), and a wide predicted range alone does not show better fit.

places.quote: A large lift means the model can maximally distinguish the best and worst risks.

That vertical distance is the model's **[[Lift|lift]]**: a large difference between the actual pure premium in the lowest and highest buckets means the model can maximally distinguish the best and worst risks

requirements.statement: Actual-to-predicted ratios that fall from above 1 in low-prediction groups to below 1 in high-prediction groups mean the model's relativities are too extreme (overfit or misspecified), so it predicts more variation than exists on new data.
Using a model with too-steep relativities overcharges the risks it rates highest and undercharges those it rates lowest, even when total premium is about adequate.

places.quote: A model that beats the current plan finds the risks the plan overcharges, which competitors can take away, and the ones it undercharges, which the insurer keeps.

requirements.statement: A scatter plot of the response against a continuous predictor shows whether the relationship is linear or curved, and its direction and spread.

places.quote: What to read off it: **direction** (up or down), **form** (straight or curved), **strength** (tight or diffuse), and **outliers** that sit away from the cloud
A scatter plot shows the direction, form and strength of a relationship and any points far from the cloud.

requirements.statement: A bar chart of exposure by level is the univariate display for a categorical variable and reveals levels with little data that cannot support their own coefficient.

places.quote: Plot exposures too, not just losses — a univariate plot of exposure by level shows where the data is thin enough that a fitted coefficient will be unstable
Plot each with a bar chart of counts or exposure by level; that is how thin levels are found before they destabilize a coefficient

requirements.statement: A correlation matrix gives pairwise correlations among continuous predictors and is used to screen for strongly related (collinear) predictor pairs, though it captures only linear relationships and only pairs.

places.quote: | **Correlation matrix** | Identify linear relationships among predictors |

A **scatter plot matrix** (all pairs of predictors) screens for *pairwise* collinearity, as the correlation matrix does — but it can miss [[Multicollinearity]], collinearity among three or more predictors when no pair is highly correlated
Detect it before fitting with a correlation matrix or a [[Scatter Plot]] matrix of the predictors

requirements.statement: A histogram shows the shape of a single variable's distribution, and for a heavily right-skewed positive variable taking logs first spreads out the bulk of the data so the shape is visible.

places.quote: For **continuous predictors**: histograms and scatter plots reveal skewness, outliers, and non-linear relationships with the response
Taking $\log$ of a positive skewed variable before plotting usually turns an uninformative spike-and-tail into a readable, near-symmetric shape
Insurance amounts are usually right-skewed, so a log scale is often the readable one

requirements.statement: Side-by-side box plots of the response by level of a categorical variable compare the response's median, spread and outliers across levels, showing whether the response differs by level.

places.quote: Box plots are read **side by side**: one box per level of a [[Categorical Predictor]] shows whether a rating variable separates the response, which is exactly the evidence needed before adding that variable to a [[Generalized Linear Model]]
| Box plot | Numerical by categorical | Median, quartiles and outliers, one box per level |
Box plots by level compare centres and spreads across groups.

requirements.statement: Gamma and inverse Gaussian distributions are continuous with strictly positive support and right skew, making them suitable for claim severity; the normal distribution allows negative values and is symmetric, and the Poisson is for counts.

places.quote: **Claim severity** — positive and right-skewed, with standard deviation roughly proportional to the mean: [[Gamma]] ($V(\mu) = \mu^2$) with a log link, weighted by claim count. The inverse Gaussian ($V(\mu) = \mu^3$) suits a heavier tail
e.g., a right-skewed, strictly positive severity favors a Gamma distribution with a log link, while integer claim counts favor a Poisson distribution
Ordinary least-squares assumes a Normal response, which can produce negative fitted severities and underweights the right skew.

requirements.statement: Variance functions of GLM distributions: normal V(μ)=1 (constant), Poisson V(μ)=μ, gamma V(μ)=μ², inverse Gaussian V(μ)=μ³, Tweedie V(μ)=μ^p.

places.quote: normal: $1$ (constant variance)
| Gamma | $\mu^2$ | $-1/\mu$ (log in practice) | Claim severity |
$$\text{Var}(Y) = \phi\,\mu^{p}, \qquad 1 < p < 2$$

requirements.statement: If the standard deviation (spread) is proportional to the mean, then the variance is proportional to the mean squared, which matches the gamma variance function (constant coefficient of variation).

places.quote: [[Gamma|gamma]]: $\mu^2$ (constant coefficient of variation)
**Claim severity** — positive and right-skewed, with standard deviation roughly proportional to the mean: [[Gamma]] ($V(\mu) = \mu^2$) with a log link, weighted by claim count.

requirements.statement: Use exploratory plots to choose a GLM distribution: a histogram shows range and skew, while box plots (spread vs median) and scatter plots (widening wedge) show how variance changes with the mean.
requirements.concept: Exploratory Data Analysis for GLM Specification

places.quote: Plot group variances against group means on log–log axes. The slope estimates $p$ in $V(\mu) = \mu^p$: $0$ for normal, $1$ for Poisson, $2$ for gamma, and between $1$ and $2$ for Tweedie.
right skew with a long tail points to [[Gamma]] or [[Lognormal Distribution|lognormal]] severity
This mean–variance plot is the practical way to pick a distribution and is a standard [[Exploratory Data Analysis]] step before fitting.

requirements.statement: A Tweedie distribution with power between 1 and 2 is a compound Poisson-gamma with a point mass at zero, used for pure premium (aggregate loss), not for positive-only severity.

places.quote: For $1 < p < 2$ it is a compound Poisson–Gamma distribution: a Poisson number of Gamma-sized claims. That gives it a point mass at zero plus a right-skewed continuous part
**Pure premium or loss cost** — mostly zeros plus a skewed positive amount: the [[Tweedie Distribution|Tweedie]] with power $1 < p < 2$ and a log link

requirements.statement: A log link keeps fitted means positive and makes the effects of predictors multiplicative.

places.quote: The **log link** is standard for insurance severity and frequency models because it guarantees positive fitted values and allows multiplicative interpretation: a unit increase in $x_j$ multiplies $\mu$ by $e^{\beta_j}$
In every case the log (or logit) link keeps the fitted mean in the range the response can take, and makes the coefficients multiplicative.

requirements.statement: The interquartile range (IQR) is the third quartile minus the first quartile, Q3 − Q1, measuring the spread of the middle half of the data.

places.quote: $$\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$$
$Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are the first and third quartiles and $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$; a value outside the fences is flagged.
$Q_1$ and $Q_3$ are the 25th and 75th percentiles and $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$ is the interquartile range

requirements.statement: To find quartiles by the median-of-halves method with odd n, locate the overall median, exclude it, and take Q1 and Q3 as the medians of the lower and upper halves of the remaining ordered values.

places.quote: this page takes the medians of the lower and upper halves (the median itself left out when $n$ is odd)

requirements.statement: The box plot outlier fences are Q1 − 1.5·IQR (lower) and Q3 + 1.5·IQR (upper); observations beyond a fence are outliers.

places.quote: $$\text{potential outlier if } x < Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} \ \text{ or } \ x > Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}$$
$$\text{Upper fence} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$$
$$x \text{ is plotted as an outlier if } x < Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} \text{ or } x > Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}$$

requirements.statement: A box plot whisker extends to the most extreme observation that is not an outlier (i.e., lies within the fences), so it ends at a data value, not at the fence, and outliers are plotted individually.

places.quote: the whiskers reach the most extreme observations that are not flagged as outliers
whiskers reach the farthest points within $1.5\,\text{IQR}$ of the box, and points beyond are drawn individually

requirements.statement: A box plot shows the median and the quartiles Q1 and Q3 (the box holds the middle half of the data), whiskers extending to the most extreme non-outlier points, and individual outliers plotted beyond the whiskers.

places.quote: The box spans the middle half of the data and the whiskers reach the most extreme observations that are not flagged as outliers.
The box runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile with a line at the median, whiskers reach the farthest points within $1.5\,\text{IQR}$ of the box, and points beyond are drawn individually.

requirements.statement: Compare side-by-side box plots across categories by looking at the location (median and box position) of each class; classes with nearly identical boxes and medians can be grouped into a single level of a categorical predictor, while a clearly shifted box suggests a separate level.

places.quote: The first two classes are not distinguished by the data and could be **grouped into one level**, saving a parameter. The third class needs its own coefficient.
The luxury class likely warrants a separate rating factor in the model (or a distinct coefficient).

requirements.statement: A level of a categorical predictor with few observations has an imprecisely estimated coefficient (large standard error), so an apparent difference should be confirmed or credibility-weighted before being fully priced.

places.quote: Plot exposures too, not just losses — a univariate plot of exposure by level shows where the data is thin enough that a fitted coefficient will be unstable
Plot each with a bar chart of counts or exposure by level; that is how thin levels are found before they destabilize a coefficient

requirements.statement: Skewness shows as asymmetry within a class (e.g., an upper whisker and upper box half longer than the lower), not as short whiskers; shorter whiskers indicate smaller scale.

places.quote: A median sitting left of centre with a long right whisker signals **right skew** — the usual shape for claim severity

requirements.statement: A few outliers are individual extreme observations and do not indicate a class's typical severity, so they are weak evidence for a different level compared with the median and box.

places.quote: Because it is built from [[Order Statistics]], it is resistant to extreme values: one enormous claim moves the maximum but not the box
**Outliers are investigated, not deleted:** An extreme claim may be real. Repeat the analysis with and without it, and drop it only with a reason that is disclosed.

requirements.statement: For a gamma-type severity response the standard deviation grows with the mean, so classes with larger medians show greater spread; differing medians indicate a difference in mean, not only in dispersion.

places.quote: The high outliers and the widening spread as the median rises indicate variance growing with the mean — a **Gamma [[Generalized Linear Model]] with a log [[Link Function]]** fits that pattern better than ordinary [[Linear Regression]].
[[Gamma|gamma]]: $\mu^2$ (constant coefficient of variation)

requirements.statement: A discrete random variable takes only a countable set of distinct values (for example, claim counts of 0, 1, 2, ...), so its distribution is described by the frequency or probability at each value.

places.quote: A **Discrete Random Variable** $X$ is a [[Random Variable]] whose possible values form a finite or countably infinite set — typically a count, such as the number of claims — so its distribution is given by a [[Probability Mass Function (PMF)|probability mass function]] $p(x) = P(X = x)$.

requirements.statement: A bar chart with one bar per value (a frequency bar chart) is the appropriate univariate display for showing how often each value of a discrete variable occurs, including the share of zeros and the tail shape.

places.quote: | [[Histogram]] | Binned counts | Overall shape, multimodality |
A histogram of a variable that is $90\%$ zeros is one tall bar; a bar chart of how often $0, 1, 2, \ldots$ occur is the right [[Univariate Plot|univariate plot]]
- **Discrete (count)** — non-negative integers: claim counts, vehicles per policy.

requirements.statement: A histogram groups a continuous variable into bins, and for a discrete variable bins that do not align with the integer values produce empty bins and a picture that depends on the bin edges.

places.quote: Applied to a discrete count variable it becomes a bar chart of the [[Probability Mass Function (PMF)|PMF]] — useful for spotting overdispersion before fitting a [[Poisson Regression]]

requirements.statement: A box plot shows the median, the quartiles Q1 and Q3 as the box, and flags as outliers points beyond 1.5 times the IQR (Q3 minus Q1) from the box.

places.quote: A **Box Plot** (box-and-whisker plot) is an [[Exploratory Data Analysis]] display that summarizes a distribution with five numbers: the minimum, first quartile $Q_1$, median $Q_2$, third quartile $Q_3$, and maximum. The box spans the middle half of the data and the whiskers reach the most extreme observations that are not flagged as outliers.

requirements.statement: When most observations are zero, the quartiles and median are all zero, so the box plot collapses to a line with IQR 0 and every nonzero value is flagged as an outlier, making it uninformative for such data.

resolution.note: applying the definitions to the stem's data: with 88% zeros Q1, the median and Q3 are all 0, so IQR = 0 and the fences flag every nonzero value; the rules used, IQR = Q3 − Q1 and the 1.5 IQR fences, are on Box Plot.

requirements.statement: A QQ plot plots the sample quantiles against the quantiles of a reference distribution to assess whether the data follow that distribution; it does not display how often each value occurs.

places.quote: A **QQ Plot** (Quantile-Quantile Plot) is a graphical diagnostic that compares the **quantiles** of a dataset against the quantiles of a theoretical distribution (or another dataset) to assess goodness of fit.

requirements.statement: A scatter plot of a variable against an arbitrary index such as a policy number shows nothing about the variable's distribution, because the index is only a label.

resolution.note: reading the stem: policy number is an arbitrary label, so plotting against it relates the count to nothing; the rule used, that a scatter plot shows the relationship between two variables, is on Scatter Plot (in reach).

requirements.statement: A spike of records at one round or extreme value (such as 99, 999, or 0) that is out of line with the rest of a smooth distribution is a typical sign of a placeholder code for missing data, and such records should be investigated, corrected, or set aside before modeling.
requirements.concept: Data Quality and Exploratory Data Analysis

places.quote: *Missing values in disguise:* an impossible zero, such as a zero dimension, is often a missing value coded as zero, which a search for missing values will not find ([[Missing Data]]).
Age $0$ is often a default written when the field was left blank, which makes it [[Missing Data|missing data]] in disguise, not a real age.

requirements.statement: A histogram of a predictor shows only the predictor's own distribution, not the shape of its relationship with the response, so linearity of the effect must be assessed from a plot of the response against the predictor or from model diagnostics.

places.quote: It is the standard first look at the relationship between a continuous predictor and the response, before any model is fitted.

requirements.statement: Box plot fences lie at Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR, where IQR = Q3 − Q1, and observations outside the fences are plotted as outliers.

places.quote: $$\text{potential outlier if } x < Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} \ \text{ or } \ x > Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}$$
$$x \text{ is plotted as an outlier if } x < Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR} \text{ or } x > Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}$$

requirements.statement: A box plot shows where outliers lie but not how many observations share a value, since repeated identical values are drawn as a single point, so a pile-up at one value is revealed by a histogram rather than a box plot.

places.quote: The five numbers behind a box plot ($\min, Q_1, Q_2, Q_3, \max$) can be identical for a symmetric unimodal sample and a symmetric **bimodal** one, and the box draws nothing between them, so a box plot cannot show two humps.

**A box plot hides the shape:** Two very different distributions, one with two clusters and one spread evenly, can give the same five numbers. Use a histogram or density plot when shape is the question.

requirements.statement: In a histogram drawn on the density scale, the area of a bar (height × bin width) equals the proportion of observations in that bin, and the total area of all bars is 1.

places.quote: On the **density scale** the bars have total area $1$, so the histogram can be overlaid directly on a fitted density; on the **count scale** the height is simply $n_j$
Drawn on the density scale, the bars have total area one, which is what lets histograms or density curves of groups of different sizes be compared.

requirements.statement: To count observations in a range spanning several bins of a density-scale histogram, sum the areas (height × width) of the bins in the range and multiply by the total number of observations.

places.quote: $$\text{bar height} = \frac{n_j}{n \cdot w} \quad \text{(density scale)}$$
The density height times the bin width, $0.00015 \times 2{,}000 = 0.30$, is the share of claims in the first bin.

requirements.statement: A Tweedie distribution with power p between 1 and 2 is a compound Poisson–gamma (a Poisson number of gamma-sized claims), giving a point mass at zero plus a continuous, right-skewed density on positive values.

places.quote: For $1 < p < 2$ it is a compound Poisson–Gamma distribution: a Poisson number of Gamma-sized claims. That gives it a point mass at zero plus a right-skewed continuous part
**Pure premium or loss cost** — mostly zeros plus a skewed positive amount: the [[Tweedie Distribution|Tweedie]] with power $1 < p < 2$ and a log link

requirements.statement: The Tweedie distribution with power between 1 and 2 is the standard single-GLM choice for modeling pure premium, since pure premium has many exact zeros and positive right-skewed amounts.

places.quote: Fitted with a **log link**, it models pure premium in one step instead of fitting [[Poisson Regression|frequency]] and severity separately
**Pure premium or loss cost** — mostly zeros plus a skewed positive amount: the [[Tweedie Distribution|Tweedie]] with power $1 < p < 2$ and a log link

requirements.statement: The gamma and inverse Gaussian distributions are defined only on positive values and have no probability mass at zero, so they suit positive severity amounts but not data with many exact zeros.

places.quote: The Gamma density is defined only for $y > 0$, but most policies have pure premium exactly $0$ — the likelihood is undefined for those rows.
is a flexible continuous distribution on $(0, \infty)$ generalizing the exponential, used to model skewed loss severities and aggregate claims.

requirements.statement: The Poisson distribution is a distribution for non-negative integer counts, so it is suited to claim frequency rather than continuous dollar amounts.

places.quote: **Claim counts** — Poisson ($V(\mu) = \mu$), or [[Negative Binomial Distribution|negative binomial]] if overdispersed

requirements.statement: A normal response is symmetric and continuous over all real values (including negatives), so it cannot represent a spike at zero together with a long right tail.

places.quote: **Continuous, roughly symmetric, constant variance** — Normal with the identity link: ordinary [[Linear Regression]]
is a symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution on $(-\infty, \infty)$

requirements.statement: A distribution that is roughly symmetric on the log scale (lognormal-like) is strongly right-skewed on the original scale.

places.quote: Taking $\log$ of a positive skewed variable before plotting usually turns an uninformative spike-and-tail into a readable, near-symmetric shape

The **Lognormal Distribution** $X \sim \text{Lognormal}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ applies when $\ln X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$. It is widely used to model insurance losses, asset prices, and any quantity that must be positive and right-skewed.

requirements.statement: The sample correlation coefficient measures only the strength and direction of linear association, so a strong non-linear relationship can have a correlation near zero.

places.quote: Strength in the *linear* direction is summarized by the [[Correlation]] coefficient $r$ — but $r$ near $0$ only rules out a linear trend, not a U-shape
**Correlation** $\rho(X, Y)$ measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two [[Random Variable|random variables]] $X$ and $Y$.

requirements.statement: Zero or near-zero correlation does not imply independence; variables can be strongly dependent (even one a function of the other) while uncorrelated.

places.quote: Zero correlation does **not** in general imply [[Independent Random Variables|independence]]: with $X$ uniform on $[-1, 1]$, $Y = X^2$ is uncorrelated with $X$ yet a function of it.
$\rho_{X,Y} = 0$ means no linear relationship, but not necessarily [[Independent Random Variables|independence]].

requirements.statement: |r| is close to 1 only when points lie close to a straight line; a tight pattern around a curve does not make |r| large.

places.quote: $\rho = 1$ is a perfect positive linear relationship, $\rho = -1$ a perfect negative one, and $\rho = 0$ no linear association.
$\rho = \pm 1$ indicates a perfect linear relationship; $\rho = 0$ indicates no linear association

requirements.statement: When a scatter plot shows a strong curved relationship between a predictor and the response, include the predictor in the model with a non-linear form such as bands (categories), a polynomial/quadratic term, or a spline, rather than dropping it or using a single linear term.

places.quote: Age is clearly predictive; it just needs the right structure — band it into a [[Categorical Predictor]], or include a quadratic term $\beta_1\,\text{age} + \beta_2\,\text{age}^2$.
**Polynomial Regression** extends [[Linear Regression]] to a non-linear relationship by adding powers of the predictor as extra predictors.

requirements.statement: A fan or wedge pattern in a plot of response against a predictor, with a linear centre and spread widening as the mean rises, indicates non-constant variance that grows with the mean, which ordinary least squares does not handle but a gamma GLM (variance proportional to the squared mean) does.

places.quote: a fan that widens to the right says the variance grows with the mean, which is an argument for a [[Generalized Linear Model]] rather than [[Linear Regression]]
[[Gamma|gamma]]: $\mu^2$ (constant coefficient of variation)

requirements.statement: A curved relationship between the response and a predictor, with a bending centre and constant spread, indicates that a transformation of the predictor, a polynomial term, or banding of the predictor is needed instead of a single linear term.

places.quote: Systematic curvature says the predictor needs a transformation ($\ln x$, $x^2$, or banding) in the [[Model Structure]]
a continuous predictor gets one coefficient, or a [[Variable Transformation|transformation]] when its effect is curved

requirements.statement: Two parallel bands of points with the same slope but different levels indicate a missing categorical variable, which is added as a categorical predictor that shifts the intercept for one group.
A shapeless cloud with no trend in the centre or spread of the response across the predictor indicates no association between the response and the predictor.
A high-leverage point is an observation with an extreme predictor value far from the others, which can pull the fitted line toward itself and substantially change the fitted slope.

places.quote: A point far out in $x$ has **high leverage** — on its own it can bend the fitted line, so it deserves a look before it is left in
A **high-leverage** point is different: its *predictor* values are unusual, measured by the leverage $h_{ii}$ (the $i$-th diagonal of the hat matrix, which depends only on the $x$ values).

requirements.statement: A high-leverage point should be investigated (for data error or a different kind of risk) before being allowed to drive the model fit.

places.quote: The first question to ask about one is always *why*: an outlier is either an **error** to be corrected, or a **real but extreme** value, such as a [[Large Loss|large loss]], that has to be kept but kept from dominating the fit.
A point far out in $x$ has **high leverage** — on its own it can bend the fitted line, so it deserves a look before it is left in

requirements.statement: The sample correlation coefficient is r = S_xy / sqrt(S_xx * S_yy), where S_xy = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ), S_xx = Σ(x−x̄)², and S_yy = Σ(y−ȳ)².

places.quote: $$r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}$$

requirements.statement: The sample mean is the sum of the observations divided by their number, and deviations from the mean are used to compute the sums of squares and cross-products.

places.quote: $S_{jj} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2$ is the centred sum of squares of predictor $x_j$
$$\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$$
$$S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(X_i - \bar{X}\right)^2$$

requirements.statement: A high-leverage point is an observation whose predictor value is far from the other predictor values; it can dominate the fitted line and the sample correlation, and a small number of observations makes this effect stronger.

places.quote: A point far out in $x$ has **high leverage** — on its own it can bend the fitted line, so it deserves a look before it is left in
A high-leverage point is different: its *predictor* values are unusual, measured by the leverage $h_{ii}$ (the $i$-th diagonal of the hat matrix, which depends only on the $x$ values).

requirements.statement: A high-leverage point pulls the least squares line toward itself, so its residual from the fitted line can be small even though it is far from the other points; a point should be investigated for its influence, not removed just for being extreme.

places.quote: A high-leverage point can be influential without having a large residual, because it pulls the fit toward itself
A point far out in $x$ has **high leverage** — on its own it can bend the fitted line, so it deserves a look before it is left in

requirements.statement: The sample correlation coefficient measures only the strength of linear association over the observed data and can be driven by a single point; a high r does not mean a steady trend across the data.

places.quote: **Correlation** $\rho(X, Y)$ measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two [[Random Variable|random variables]] $X$ and $Y$.
Strength in the *linear* direction is summarized by the [[Correlation]] coefficient $r$ — but $r$ near $0$ only rules out a linear trend, not a U-shape

requirements.statement: R-squared (the square of r in simple linear regression) is a single summary of the proportion of variation explained over the whole data set; it does not describe the fit within subsets or at each value of the predictor.

places.quote: **R-Squared** ($R^2$), also called the **coefficient of determination**, measures the proportion of total variance in the response variable $Y$ that is explained by the model.

requirements.statement: Correlation or regression association does not imply causation.
Conclusions from a regression should not be extrapolated to predictor ranges where there are no observations, because the data cannot show the pattern there.

places.quote: Data far from the origin say nothing about whether the line really runs through it.
A significant slope confirms there is a trend; it does not validate extrapolating the straight line several years out.

requirements.statement: Assess a regression or correlation by examining the data points (e.g., recomputing the correlation or slope with a suspect point excluded) rather than relying on r alone.

places.quote: A point is **influential** when removing it would change the fitted coefficients materially.
Dropping a variable on the strength of $r$ alone is the classic scatter-plot mistake.

requirements.statement: When the number of predictors p is at least the number of observations n, least squares can fit the training data exactly (RSS = 0, R^2 = 1) regardless of whether the predictors are related to the response, so training fit is not evidence of a good model.

places.quote: Once $p \ge n$, least squares and other classical methods fit the training data perfectly whether or not any real relationship exists, so they overfit badly.

requirements.statement: Training-set measures such as RSS and R^2 always improve (or do not worsen) as predictors are added, so they are unreliable for assessing model fit and choosing among models.

places.quote: $R^2$ **always increases** (or stays the same) when predictors are added, even if they are irrelevant

Training RSS, [[R-Squared]], p-values and the usual fit measures are useless as evidence: adding features unrelated to the response drives $R^2$ to $1$ and training MSE to $0$, while test MSE explodes.

requirements.statement: In high-dimensional settings (p > n), less flexible methods such as the lasso, ridge regression, or forward stepwise selection are preferred, because shrinkage keeps the fit from interpolating the data.

places.quote: Less flexible fitting methods: forward stepwise selection ([[Variable Selection]]), ridge regression and the lasso ([[Regularization]]), and [[Principal Components Regression]].

requirements.statement: Cross-validation can be used to select the lasso tuning parameter (penalty) and to estimate the test (prediction) error of the fitted model, even when p > n.

places.quote: **Cross-Validation** estimates how well a model predicts **new** data by repeatedly holding part of the sample out of the fit and scoring the model on it.
Report performance on an independent test set or by cross-validation ([[Test Error]]), never on the training data.

requirements.statement: The error variance estimate used in Cp, AIC, and BIC is sigma-hat^2 = RSS/(n - p - 1).
requirements.concept: Estimating Error Variance in Linear Regression

places.quote: $$\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - p - 1}$$

requirements.statement: Cp, AIC, BIC, and adjusted R^2 are unreliable when p is close to or exceeds n, because the error variance estimate becomes near zero or undefined.

places.quote: $C_p$, [[AIC]] and [[BIC]] are unreliable because $\hat\sigma^2$ is, and adjusted $R^2$ can be made $1$.

requirements.statement: Training R^2 never decreases as predictors are added and reaches 1 when the number of coefficients equals the number of observations, so a high training R^2 does not show predictive ability, especially when p > n.

places.quote: adding features unrelated to the response drives $R^2$ to $1$ and training MSE to $0$, while test MSE explodes.
$R^2$ **always increases** (or stays the same) when predictors are added, even if they are irrelevant

requirements.statement: Adjusted R^2 penalizes only the number of predictors in the final model, not the search over all candidate predictors, so after selection from many candidates it remains optimistic.

places.quote: $C_p$, [[AIC]] and [[BIC]] are unreliable because $\hat\sigma^2$ is, and adjusted $R^2$ can be made $1$.
**Adjusted $R^2$** corrects for this by penalizing for the number of predictors $p$:

requirements.statement: P-values and standard errors from a fit whose features were selected because they fit the same data are not valid; among many candidate features, noise features can appear highly significant by chance.

places.quote: Training RSS, [[R-Squared]], p-values and the usual fit measures are useless as evidence

requirements.statement: AIC, BIC and Cp rely on an error variance estimate that is unreliable when p is large relative to n, and they are computed on the same data used for selection, so they do not reliably indicate test performance in high dimensions.

places.quote: $C_p$, [[AIC]] and [[BIC]] are unreliable because $\hat\sigma^2$ is, and adjusted $R^2$ can be made $1$.
[[AIC]] and [[BIC]] instead adjust training error for complexity.
It measures test error directly, rather than penalizing complexity indirectly as [[AIC]] and [[BIC]] do.

requirements.statement: Test error on held-out data estimates performance on new observations only if the held-out data were set aside before any feature selection or fitting, so the selection could not adapt to them.

places.quote: Each part can judge a step only if that step has never seen it, so every reuse of a held-out set to make a decision turns it, gradually, into training data.

Everything that learns from the response must use the training data only. That includes [[Variable Selection|selecting variables]], banding them, and tuning. Otherwise the holdout has already influenced the model

requirements.statement: Cross-validation gives a valid estimate of test error with feature selection only if the whole selection procedure is repeated within each fold.

places.quote: Every step that touches the response — [[Variable Selection]], banding a variable by its indicated relativities, tuning a penalty — must sit **inside** the fold, or the held-out data has already influenced the fit and the CV error is optimistic
Cross-validation uses every record for testing, but it only gives an honest estimate if every modeling step, including variable selection, is repeated inside each fold.

requirements.statement: A proportional odds (cumulative logit) model for an ordinal response models ln(γ_j/(1−γ_j)) = θ_j + βx, where γ_j = P(Y ≤ j) is the cumulative probability up to category j and θ_j are increasing cut-point intercepts.

places.quote: The usual form is the **proportional odds** (cumulative logit) model, which applies the logit [[Link Function]] to each $\gamma_j$ and gives every cut-point its own intercept $\theta_j$ but one common set of slopes $\boldsymbol\beta$.
The **proportional odds** (cumulative logit) model applies the logit to the cumulative probabilities $\gamma_j = \Pr(Y \le j)$, with an intercept for each cut-point but one set of slopes:

requirements.statement: In the proportional odds model the slope coefficients β are the same for every cut-point, so the cut-point intercepts θ_j cancel when comparing two covariate settings and the odds ratio of cumulative odds is the same at every cut-point.

places.quote: A covariate multiplies the odds of "category $j$ or below" by the *same* factor $e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta}$ at every cut-point.
A change in the covariates multiplies the odds of a response in category $j$ or below by the same factor, $e^{\Delta\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}}$, for every $j$ — hence the name.

requirements.statement: In the cumulative logit model, the odds ratio of being at or below category j for covariate x+1 versus x equals e^β, obtained by exponentiating the model: γ_j/(1−γ_j) = e^{θ_j} e^{βx}.

places.quote: Exponentiating gives $\gamma_j/(1-\gamma_j) = e^{\theta_j}\,e^{\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta}$.
A change in the covariates multiplies the odds of a response in category $j$ or below by the same factor, $e^{\Delta\mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}}$, for every $j$ — hence the name.

requirements.statement: A negative β in the form ln(γ_j/(1−γ_j)) = θ_j + βx lowers the cumulative odds and probability of low categories and shifts the response toward higher categories; the sign interpretation reverses if software uses the form θ_j − βx.

places.quote: In the form above a positive $\beta$ raises the odds of the *lower* categories. Output may instead report the latent-variable coefficients, with the model written $\theta_j - \mathbf{x}^\top\boldsymbol\beta^*$; there a positive coefficient shifts the response toward the *higher* categories.

requirements.statement: Individual category probabilities are obtained by differencing cumulative probabilities: P(Y=j) = γ_j − γ_{j−1}, with γ_j = e^{θ_j+βx}/(1+e^{θ_j+βx}) and the top category equal to 1 − γ_{J−1}.

places.quote: $$\pi_j = \gamma_j - \gamma_{j-1}$$

requirements.statement: The odds ratio multiplies cumulative odds, not individual category probabilities, so category probabilities are not simply scaled by e^β.

places.quote: Attorney involvement multiplies the **odds** of referral by $2.23$ but the **probability** by only $1.82$.

requirements.statement: In the proportional odds (cumulative logit) model, the cumulative probability γ_j = P(Y ≤ j) satisfies ln(γ_j/(1−γ_j)) = θ_j + β·x, with a separate intercept θ_j for each cut-point and common slope coefficients β across all categories.

places.quote: The usual form is the **proportional odds** (cumulative logit) model, which applies the logit [[Link Function]] to each $\gamma_j$ and gives every cut-point its own intercept $\theta_j$ but one common set of slopes $\boldsymbol\beta$.
The **proportional odds** (cumulative logit) model applies the logit to the cumulative probabilities $\gamma_j = \Pr(Y \le j)$, with an intercept for each cut-point but one set of slopes:

requirements.statement: To get a cumulative probability from a logit model, compute the linear predictor θ_j + β·x and invert the logit: γ_j = 1/(1 + e^{−(θ_j + β·x)}).

places.quote: | Logit | $\ln\!\frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ | $\frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta}$ | Binomial (binary outcomes) |

requirements.statement: In an ordinal response with ordered categories, the probability of a single category is the difference of adjacent cumulative probabilities: P(Y = j) = γ_j − γ_{j−1}, with γ_0 = 0.

places.quote: $j = 1, \dots, J-1$, with $\gamma_0 = 0$ and $\gamma_J = 1$; $\pi_j = P(Y = j \mid \mathbf{x})$.

requirements.statement: The probability of the highest category equals the complement of the last cumulative probability: P(Y = k) = 1 − γ_{k−1}, since γ_k = 1.
The deviance of a log-linear model for a contingency table is compared with a chi-squared distribution whose degrees of freedom equal the number of cells minus the number of fitted parameters.

places.quote: The [[Deviance]] of the additive model, $D = 2\sum y_{ij}\ln(y_{ij}/\hat\mu_{ij})$, is approximately $\chi^2$ with $(I-1)(J-1)$ degrees of freedom.
in large samples a model that fits has $D \approx \chi^2_{n-p}$

requirements.statement: In an I by J table, the independence model ln(mu_ij) = intercept + row effect + column effect has I + J - 1 parameters, so its deviance has (I-1)(J-1) degrees of freedom.

places.quote: The [[Deviance]] of the additive model, $D = 2\sum y_{ij}\ln(y_{ij}/\hat\mu_{ij})$, is approximately $\chi^2$ with $(I-1)(J-1)$ degrees of freedom.
tests whether two classifications are independent, on $(k-1)(m-1)$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: Conditioning independent Poisson cell counts on their total gives a multinomial distribution, so a log-linear model with an intercept gives the same fitted counts (row total times column total divided by grand total under independence) under Poisson or multinomial sampling.
requirements.concept: Poisson and Multinomial Sampling for Contingency Tables

places.quote: Conditioning Poisson counts on their total gives the multinomial, and a model that includes those margins reproduces them exactly. So the Poisson log-linear fit gives the same fitted values and tests in each case.

requirements.statement: In a three-way table, the model AB + C includes the A-B interaction but no term linking C to A or B, so (A, B) is jointly independent of C.
requirements.concept: Three-Way Contingency Tables and Log-Linear Model Hierarchy

places.quote: $A + B + C$ is complete independence, and $AB + C$ means $A$ and $B$ are associated but jointly independent of $C$.

requirements.statement: The deviance of a Poisson log-linear (GLM) model measures its lack of fit relative to the saturated model, which has zero deviance and one parameter per cell.

places.quote: It compares the fitted model to the **saturated model** (a model with one parameter per observation, achieving perfect fit).
The second block is the **saturated** model, which reproduces every count.

requirements.statement: Test the goodness of fit of a log-linear model by comparing its deviance with the chi-squared critical value whose degrees of freedom equal the model's residual degrees of freedom; a deviance below the critical value means the model fits.

places.quote: in large samples a model that fits has $D \approx \chi^2_{n-p}$
The [[Deviance]] of the additive model, $D = 2\sum y_{ij}\ln(y_{ij}/\hat\mu_{ij})$, is approximately $\chi^2$ with $(I-1)(J-1)$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: Compare nested models by taking the difference in deviances and comparing it with the chi-squared critical value on the difference in degrees of freedom; a significant drop means the extra term is needed, otherwise it can be dropped.

places.quote: for nested models, $\dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\phi} \approx \chi^2_{\Delta p}$ when $\phi$ is known (large samples).
For a GLM this statistic is the **difference in deviances divided by the dispersion**
For Poisson and binomial $\phi = 1$, so the raw change in deviance is compared with $\chi^2$;

requirements.statement: A larger model always fits at least as well (has lower or equal deviance) as a model nested within it, so the lowest deviance alone is not a valid selection criterion; parsimony requires keeping only terms that significantly improve fit.

places.quote: Adding terms always improves in-sample fit but risks overfitting
Adding any predictor lowers deviance.
not by raw RSS, $R^2$ or deviance, which always improve as predictors are added

requirements.statement: In a hierarchical log-linear model for a three-way table, the absence of a term linking two variables (e.g. no XY term in XZ + YZ) means X and Y are conditionally independent given the third variable Z.
The degrees of freedom of the difference between two nested log-linear models equal the difference of their residual degrees of freedom, which is the number of parameters removed.
requirements.concept: Degrees of Freedom in Log-Linear Models

places.quote: for nested models, $\dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\phi} \approx \chi^2_{\Delta p}$ when $\phi$ is known (large samples).
is asymptotically $\chi^2$ with degrees of freedom equal to the number of added parameters.

requirements.statement: A quasi-Poisson model keeps the Poisson mean structure and log link but specifies Var(Y) = φμ, with φ a dispersion parameter that allows for overdispersion.

places.quote: The analyst specifies only how the mean depends on the predictors and how the variance depends on the mean, up to a constant of proportionality $\phi$.
estimate $\phi$ (quasi-Poisson, which inflates standard errors by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$ but leaves $\hat\beta$ unchanged)

requirements.statement: In a quasi-Poisson fit the dispersion parameter cancels from the estimating equations (IRLS weights are all divided by the same φ), so the coefficient estimates equal the Poisson GLM estimates.

places.quote: For [[Poisson Regression]] with $\text{Var}(Y) = \phi\mu$, $\phi$ cancels out of the weighted least-squares step. So $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is *exactly* the Poisson estimate, and $\phi$ is estimated alongside it.
estimate $\phi$ (quasi-Poisson, which inflates standard errors by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$ but leaves $\hat\beta$ unchanged)

requirements.statement: Under quasi-Poisson the covariance matrix of the coefficient estimates is φ times the Poisson covariance matrix, so each standard error is multiplied by √φ.

places.quote: Only the variances change: $\text{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \phi(X^\top W X)^{-1}$, so standard errors are multiplied by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$.

$\phi$ does **not** affect the fitted coefficients $\hat\beta$ — it scales their standard errors by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$, and so changes every p-value and [[Confidence Interval]] in [[Parameter Estimate Tables]]

requirements.statement: The dispersion parameter is estimated as Pearson's chi-square statistic divided by the residual degrees of freedom.

places.quote: $$\hat\phi = \frac{X^2}{n-p}$$
Two estimators are in common use — the Pearson $\chi^2$ statistic over degrees of freedom (above) and the unscaled residual [[Deviance]] over degrees of freedom, $D/(n-p)$.

requirements.statement: The Wald (z or t) test statistic for a coefficient is the estimate divided by its standard error.

places.quote: | **z-value** or **t-value** | $\hat{\beta} / \text{SE}(\hat{\beta})$; test statistic for $H_0: \beta = 0$ |
The Wald test (coefficient over its standard error, as printed in [[Parameter Estimate Tables]]) and the score test are asymptotically equivalent to the LRT.

requirements.statement: In a quasi-Poisson (quasi-likelihood) model, the dispersion parameter is estimated as Pearson's chi-square statistic divided by the residual degrees of freedom (n - p).

places.quote: $$\hat\phi = \frac{X^2}{n-p}$$
$$\hat\phi = \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{w_i\,(y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2}{V(\hat\mu_i)} \qquad \text{(Pearson estimate)}$$

requirements.statement: The F statistic for comparing nested quasi-likelihood GLMs is the drop in deviance divided by the difference in residual degrees of freedom, then divided by the estimated dispersion: F = [(D_0 - D_1)/(df_0 - df_1)] / phi-hat.

places.quote: Nested models use the drop in [[Deviance]] per degree of freedom divided by $\hat\phi$, which is compared with an $F$ distribution.
When $\phi$ is estimated, use $F = \dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\Delta p\,\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$ on $(\Delta p,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom

requirements.statement: The quasi-likelihood F statistic is compared with an F distribution with numerator df equal to the number of added parameters (difference in residual df) and denominator df equal to the residual df of the larger model; a large F indicates the added variable is significant.

places.quote: When $\phi$ is estimated, use $F = \dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\Delta p\,\hat\phi_{\text{full}}}$ on $(\Delta p,\ n - p_{\text{full}})$ degrees of freedom
**GLMs:** to test $k$ added parameters, $\dfrac{D_S - D_B}{k\,\hat{\phi}_B}$ is compared with $F(k,\ n - p_B)$

requirements.statement: The difference in residual degrees of freedom between nested models equals the number of additional parameters, so a categorical variable with k levels adds k-1 parameters.
requirements.concept: Residual Degrees of Freedom in GLMs

places.quote: The change **scaled by the dispersion** $\phi$, $[D_{\text{small}} - D_{\text{big}}]/\phi$, is asymptotically $\chi^2$ with degrees of freedom equal to the number of added parameters.
$r$ is the number of **restrictions** — the difference in free parameters between the full and reduced models

requirements.statement: Quadratic discriminant analysis assumes that within each class k the predictors follow a multivariate normal distribution with its own class-specific mean vector and its own full covariance matrix Σ_k.

places.quote: **Quadratic Discriminant Analysis** (QDA) is a classifier that assumes the predictors in each class $k$ are multivariate normal with their own mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu_k$ **and their own covariance matrix** $\boldsymbol\Sigma_k$.

requirements.statement: Naive Bayes assumes that within each class the predictors are independent, so the joint density factors as f_k(x) = f_k1(x_1) × ... × f_kp(x_p), which sets all within-class covariances to zero.

places.quote: It assumes that, **within each class, the $p$ predictors are independent**, so each class's joint density factors into one-dimensional densities that are easy to estimate.
[[Naive Bayes]] with normal predictors is QDA with each $\boldsymbol\Sigma_k$ restricted to be **diagonal** (predictors independent within a class).

requirements.statement: In naive Bayes, a qualitative predictor's within-class density f_kj is estimated as the proportion of class-k training observations at each level of that predictor.

places.quote: For a qualitative predictor, use the proportion of class-$k$ training observations at each level.

requirements.statement: Naive Bayes and QDA are generative classifiers: they model the distribution of X within each class and the priors π_k, then obtain P(Y=k | X=x) via Bayes' theorem, whereas logistic regression is discriminative and models the posterior directly.

places.quote: $$P(Y = k \mid X = \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\pi_k\,f_{k1}(x_1) \cdots f_{kp}(x_p)}{\sum_{l=1}^{K} \pi_l\,f_{l1}(x_1) \cdots f_{lp}(x_p)}$$
It plugs estimates of these and the class priors into [[Bayes Theorem]] and assigns an observation to the class whose **discriminant function** $\delta_k(\mathbf{x})$ is largest.
$$\ln\!\left(\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p$$

requirements.statement: The QDA discriminant function is quadratic in x, so the decision boundary between classes is a quadratic curve or surface, in contrast with LDA, whose common covariance matrix gives a linear boundary.

places.quote: $\mathbf{x}$ enters $\delta_k$ **quadratically**, hence the name, so the boundary between two classes is a quadratic curve or surface.

requirements.statement: Naive Bayes with normal marginal densities is equivalent to QDA with diagonal class covariance matrices, so when a predictor's variance differs by class its boundary retains a squared term for that predictor and is curved (without cross-product terms).

places.quote: With normal $f_{kj}$, it amounts to QDA with a **diagonal** class covariance matrix.
$$\delta_k(x) = -\frac{(x - \mu_k)^2}{2\sigma_k^2} - \ln\sigma_k + \ln\pi_k$$

requirements.statement: Naive Bayes posterior: P(class | x) is proportional to the class prior times the product of the per-feature conditional probabilities P(x_j | class), assuming features are conditionally independent given the class.

places.quote: $$P(Y = k \mid X = \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\pi_k\,f_{k1}(x_1) \cdots f_{kp}(x_p)}{\sum_{l=1}^{K} \pi_l\,f_{l1}(x_1) \cdots f_{lp}(x_p)}$$

requirements.statement: For a binary feature that is absent in the observation, use the complement (1 minus the within-class rate of the flag being present) as that feature's conditional probability in each class.

places.quote: The "no attorney" rates are $1 - 0.30 = 0.70$ for fraud and $1 - 0.05 = 0.95$ for legitimate claims.
$$P(A^c \mid B) = 1 - P(A \mid B)$$

requirements.statement: Normalize the class-wise products (prior times likelihood) by dividing each by their sum over all classes to obtain the posterior probability of the class.

places.quote: $$= \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i} P(E \mid H_i)\,P(H_i)}$$
The posterior probabilities are $0.12281/0.20513 = 0.5987$ (good) and $0.08232/0.20513 = 0.4013$ (bad).

requirements.statement: For one predictor with class-specific normal densities, the QDA discriminant function is delta_k(x) = -(x-mu_k)^2/(2 sigma_k^2) - ln(sigma_k) + ln(pi_k), where mu_k, sigma_k^2 and pi_k are the class mean, variance and prior probability.

places.quote: $$\delta_k(x) = -\frac{(x - \mu_k)^2}{2\sigma_k^2} - \ln\sigma_k + \ln\pi_k$$

requirements.statement: QDA assumes each class has its own normal distribution with its own variance (covariance matrix), unlike LDA which assumes a shared variance, so the variance-dependent terms do not cancel between classes.

places.quote: assumes the predictors in each class $k$ are multivariate normal with their own mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu_k$ **and their own covariance matrix** $\boldsymbol\Sigma_k$.

requirements.statement: Convert discriminant values to posterior class probabilities by noting exp(delta_k(x)) is proportional to pi_k f_k(x), so P(class k | x) = exp(delta_k) / sum over classes of exp(delta_j).

places.quote: $$= \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{\displaystyle\sum_{i} P(E \mid H_i)\,P(H_i)}$$
$$P(Y = k \mid X = \mathbf{x}) = \frac{\pi_k\,f_{k1}(x_1) \cdots f_{kp}(x_p)}{\sum_{l=1}^{K} \pi_l\,f_{l1}(x_1) \cdots f_{lp}(x_p)}$$

requirements.statement: The Bayes posterior for a class combines the prior probability with the class density, so ignoring the priors or the density's 1/sigma factor gives wrong posterior probabilities.

places.quote: updating the prior probability $P(H)$ of a hypothesis to the posterior probability $P(H \mid E)$ after observing evidence $E$.
A density, not a probability, is used for the quantitative predictor. The common $dx$ cancels between numerator and denominator.

requirements.statement: Quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA) assumes each class has its own multivariate normal distribution with a class-specific mean vector and covariance matrix, and classifies to the class with the largest discriminant function, which includes the prior term ln(pi_k).

places.quote: **Quadratic Discriminant Analysis** (QDA) is a classifier that assumes the predictors in each class $k$ are multivariate normal with their own mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu_k$ **and their own covariance matrix** $\boldsymbol\Sigma_k$.

requirements.statement: QDA's decision boundary is quadratic in the predictors, whereas LDA, which assumes a covariance matrix shared by all classes, has a linear boundary.

places.quote: $\mathbf{x}$ enters $\delta_k$ **quadratically**, hence the name, so the boundary between two classes is a quadratic curve or surface.

requirements.statement: A covariance matrix for p predictors has p(p+1)/2 distinct variance and covariance parameters, and QDA estimates one such matrix per class (plus p means per class).

places.quote: Each class needs its own $p(p+1)/2$ covariance parameters, or $Kp(p+1)/2$ in all.

requirements.statement: Estimating many parameters from few observations gives a high-variance fit; a more flexible model such as QDA has lower bias but higher variance, so with small class sample sizes relative to p a more restricted model (LDA or naive Bayes) tends to give lower test error.

places.quote: QDA is preferred when the training set is large or a common covariance is clearly untenable; with few observations the shared-covariance model is usually the better bet ([[Bias-Variance Tradeoff]]).
More data lowers variance without touching bias, so a complex model that overfits at $n = 500$ may be exactly right at $n = 50{,}000$
The method often does well, especially when $n$ is not large relative to $p$.

requirements.statement: Naive Bayes assumes predictors are independent within each class (a diagonal covariance matrix in the Gaussian case), which introduces bias but reduces the number of parameters and variance.

places.quote: [[Naive Bayes]] with normal predictors is QDA with each $\boldsymbol\Sigma_k$ restricted to be **diagonal** (predictors independent within a class).
It assumes that, **within each class, the $p$ predictors are independent**, so each class's joint density factors into one-dimensional densities that are easy to estimate.

requirements.statement: A polynomial regression of degree d is an ordinary linear model in the predictors x, x^2, ..., x^d because it is linear in the coefficients, so it is fit by ordinary least squares rather than non-linear methods.

places.quote: Its coefficients are still estimated by least squares, because it is a standard linear model in the predictors $x_i, x_i^2, \dots, x_i^d$.

requirements.statement: A lower-degree polynomial model is nested in a higher-degree one (extra coefficients set to zero), so least squares on the larger model cannot have a higher training RSS; training error never increases with added flexibility.

places.quote: Training MSE falls every time flexibility is added, because a model with as many free parameters as observations can reproduce them exactly.
Training error keeps falling as a model gets more flexible, while error on new data falls and then rises, a U-shape.

resolution.quote: always increases** (or stays the same) when predictors are added, even if they are irrelevant
resolution.note: passage on R-Squared (linked): R^2 never falls as predictors are added, i.e. training RSS never rises when the degree-4 model is nested in degree 12; the check's miss.

requirements.statement: A high-degree polynomial imposes a single global shape and is very flexible, so it tends to oscillate wildly near the boundaries of the data where observations are sparse; degrees above 3 or 4 are unusual.

places.quote: Values of $d$ above 3 or 4 are unusual. At high degree the curve becomes overly flexible and can take very strange shapes, especially near the boundary of $X$.

requirements.statement: Polynomial regression is a global method: changing data in one region changes every coefficient and so the whole fitted curve, unlike local methods such as step functions or splines.

places.quote: A polynomial imposes one global shape on the whole range of $X$.

requirements.statement: In polynomial regression the individual coefficients of powers of x are not interpretable as separate marginal effects, since x, x^2, x^3 cannot change independently; only the fitted function matters.

places.quote: The individual coefficients are rarely of interest. What matters is the fitted function across a grid of $x$ values.

requirements.statement: The variance of the fitted value at x0 is Var(f̂(x0)) = ℓ0ᵀ Ĉ ℓ0, where ℓ0 = (1, x0, ..., x0^d) and Ĉ is the coefficient covariance matrix, so it depends on x0 and is typically largest near the ends of the range.
requirements.concept: Pointwise Standard Error of a Regression Fit

places.quote: $$\operatorname{Var}\big[\hat f(x_0)\big] = \ell_0^T \hat{\mathbf{C}}\, \ell_0$$

requirements.statement: The variance of a linear combination of estimated regression coefficients, ℓ'β̂, is ℓ' Ĉ ℓ, where Ĉ is the estimated covariance matrix of the coefficient estimates.

places.quote: $$\operatorname{Var}\big[\hat f(x_0)\big] = \ell_0^T \hat{\mathbf{C}}\, \ell_0$$
$$\text{Var}(L) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2\,\text{Var}(X_i) + 2\sum_{i < j} c_i c_j\,\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$$

requirements.statement: Expanding the quadratic form ℓ' Ĉ ℓ gives each diagonal variance weighted by the square of its ℓ term and each off-diagonal covariance weighted by twice the product of its two ℓ terms.
requirements.concept: Variance of a Linear Combination of Random Variables

places.quote: each diagonal entry is weighted by the square of its $\ell_0$ term and each off-diagonal entry by twice the product of its two terms:
$$\text{Var}(L) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^2\,\text{Var}(X_i) + 2\sum_{i < j} c_i c_j\,\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$$

requirements.statement: For a polynomial regression fitted value at x, the fitted function equals ℓ'β̂ with ℓ = (1, x, x²), so its variance is found by applying ℓ to the coefficient covariance matrix.

places.quote: $\hat f(x_0) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_0 + \cdots + \hat\beta_d x_0^d$ is the fit at a point $x_0$, and $\ell_0^T = (1, x_0, x_0^2, \dots, x_0^d)$.

requirements.statement: The standard error of an estimate is the square root of its estimated variance.

places.quote: The standard error of $\hat f(x_0)$ is the square root of the variance above.

requirements.statement: An approximate 95% pointwise confidence band for a fitted value is the estimate plus or minus 2 standard errors (about 1.96 under normal approximation).

places.quote: Computing it at each $x_0$ and plotting $\hat f(x_0) \pm 2\,\text{SE}$ gives an approximate 95% [[Confidence Interval]] for normally distributed errors.
$$\hat\theta \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat\theta)}$$

requirements.statement: A step-function regression converts a continuous predictor into indicator variables C_k(X) = I(c_k ≤ X < c_{k+1}) for cutpoints c_k, so each cutpoint belongs to the bin it starts (lower bound inclusive, upper bound exclusive).

places.quote: A step function is a basis-function model with $b_j(x_i) = I(c_j \le x_i < c_{j+1})$.
the [[Step Function]] ($b_j(x_i) = I(c_j \le x_i < c_{j+1})$) are special cases.

requirements.statement: In a least squares fit with an intercept and one indicator per bin except the first, the fitted value in each bin equals the mean of the responses in that bin.

places.quote: With only the intercept and two indicators, each bin's fitted value is just the mean of the claims in that bin:

requirements.statement: In a regression with indicator variables for all categories but one, the intercept estimate equals the mean response of the omitted reference category, and each indicator coefficient equals that category's mean minus the reference category's mean.

places.quote: When $X < c_1$ all of them are zero, so $\beta_0$ is the mean value of $Y$ for $X < c_1$.
With a single indicator in the model, its coefficient is simply the difference between the group means.

requirements.statement: Indicator (dummy) variables for categories of a binned predictor take value 1 if the observation falls in the bin and 0 otherwise, so a step-function regression fits a separate mean for each bin.
requirements.concept: Dummy Variables (Indicator Variables) in Linear Regression

places.quote: $I(\cdot)$ is the indicator function: $1$ if the condition is true and $0$ otherwise. These are dummy variables.

requirements.statement: If the indicators for all categories of a variable are included along with an intercept, they sum to the intercept column, so the design matrix is not of full rank (perfect collinearity, the dummy variable trap).

places.quote: For any $X$, $C_0(X) + C_1(X) + \cdots + C_K(X) = 1$, because $X$ falls in exactly one of the $K + 1$ intervals.
The classic case is the dummy-variable trap — an intercept plus an indicator for *every* level.

requirements.statement: When software reports NA for a coefficient, that column was dropped as linearly dependent on the others, and its category becomes the reference level absorbed into the intercept.

places.quote: the omitted level is the **reference level**, absorbed into the intercept
Software either refuses or silently drops one column, so always check which level ended up as the base.

requirements.statement: With a reference category, the intercept equals the reference category's mean response and each other category's coefficient equals that category's mean minus the reference mean.
requirements.concept: Interpretation of Regression Coefficients for Categorical Predictors

places.quote: When $X < c_1$ all of them are zero, so $\beta_0$ is the mean value of $Y$ for $X < c_1$.
With a single indicator in the model, its coefficient is simply the difference between the group means.

requirements.statement: To predict for an observation, add the intercept and the coefficients of the indicators equal to 1 for that observation, ignoring those equal to 0.
requirements.concept: Prediction from a Fitted Linear Regression Model

places.quote: For $c_j \le X < c_{j+1}$ the model predicts $\beta_0 + \beta_j$, so $\beta_j$ is the average increase in the response for that bin relative to $X < c_1$.

requirements.statement: The estimated standard error of a linear contrast C = sum c_i * mu_i in one-way ANOVA is sqrt(MSE * sum(c_i^2 / n_i)), so a pairwise difference of two group means has standard error sqrt(MSE * (1/n_i + 1/n_j)).

places.quote: $$s_{\hat{C}}^2 = \hat\sigma^2 \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{c_i^2}{n_i}$$

requirements.statement: Bonferroni method: to achieve family-wise error rate alpha across g simultaneous intervals, build each interval with individual error rate alpha/g, using the t critical value with two-sided area alpha/g.

places.quote: Each interval is built at confidence $1 - \alpha/g$ (each test at level $\alpha/g$).

requirements.statement: The number of pairwise comparisons among k groups is k(k-1)/2, and this is the value of g used in the Bonferroni adjustment when all pairwise differences are compared.

resolution.quote: counts the number of ways to select $k$ objects from $n$ distinct objects when order does not matter
resolution.note: passage on Combination (Exam P prerequisite): the number of pairs among k groups is k choose 2; g in the Bonferroni adjustment is that count by r2; the check's miss.

requirements.statement: A confidence interval for a contrast has half-width equal to the t critical value (with the error degrees of freedom of the ANOVA) times the contrast's estimated standard error.

places.quote: The general form is $\hat\theta \pm (\text{critical value}) \times \text{SE}(\hat\theta)$, where the critical value comes from the estimator's [[Sampling Distribution]]
The three procedures below share the form $\hat{C} \pm (\text{multiplier}) \times s_{\hat{C}}$ and differ in the multiplier.

requirements.statement: The standard error of a contrast of group means in one-way ANOVA is sqrt(sigma-hat^2 * sum(c_i^2/n_i)); for a pairwise difference with equal group sizes n it is sqrt(sigma-hat^2 * (2/n)).

places.quote: s_{\hat{C}}^2 = \hat\sigma^2 \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{c_i^2}{n_i}

requirements.statement: The Scheffé simultaneous interval for a contrast is the estimate plus or minus sqrt((k-1) F_{alpha; k-1, N-k}) times the contrast's standard error, where k is the number of groups.

places.quote: \hat{C} \pm \sqrt{(k - 1)\,F_{\alpha;\,k - 1,\,N - k}}\; s_{\hat{C}}

requirements.statement: The Tukey simultaneous interval for all pairwise differences with equal group sizes n is the difference plus or minus q_{alpha; k, N-k} * sqrt(sigma-hat^2 / n), using the studentized range percentile.

places.quote: \bar{y}_i - \bar{y}_j \pm q_{\alpha;\,k,\,N - k}\;\hat\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}

requirements.statement: The Bonferroni interval for g comparisons uses a t percentile with two-sided area alpha/g, giving at least (1-alpha) family-wise confidence.

places.quote: \hat{C}_i \pm t_{\alpha/(2g),\,N - k}\; s_{\hat{C}_i}

requirements.statement: A comparison chosen after looking at the data (e.g., the largest difference of means) is effectively the maximum over all pairwise comparisons, so an ordinary per-comparison t interval understates the error rate and a family-wise method covering all pairs is required.

places.quote: covers every contrast at once, including ones chosen after looking at the data

requirements.statement: For all pairwise differences with equal group sizes, Tukey's method is exact and gives the narrowest interval; Bonferroni is conservative and wider, and Scheffé, which covers all contrasts, is widest, but Scheffé is appropriate when non-pairwise contrasts are of interest.

places.quote: Coverage is exactly $1 - \alpha$ for equal sizes and conservative for unequal sizes. When all pairwise differences are wanted, Tukey gives narrower intervals than Bonferroni or Scheffé.

requirements.statement: A simultaneous confidence interval for a difference of means indicates a significant difference if it excludes zero, i.e., if the observed difference exceeds the half-width.

places.quote: The interval $(0.105,\ 0.735)$ excludes 0, consistent with rejecting $\beta_1 = 0$ at 5%.
Because $8{,}000$ lies inside the interval, a two-sided test of $H_0: \mu = 8{,}000$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ would **not** reject.

requirements.statement: A chi-squared distribution with k degrees of freedom is the distribution of a sum of k squared independent standard normal random variables.

places.quote: The **Chi-Squared Distribution** $\chi^2(n)$ with $n$ degrees of freedom is the distribution of the sum of squares of $n$ independent standard [[Normal Distribution|normal]] variables.

requirements.statement: For a normal random sample, (X_i - mu)/sigma are independent standard normals, so the sum of squared deviations from the true mean divided by sigma^2 is chi-squared with n degrees of freedom.
requirements.concept: Sampling Distributions from a Normal Population

places.quote: Its CDF has no closed form and is evaluated via the standard normal $Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma \sim N(0,1)$ using $\Phi$ tables
The **Chi-Squared Distribution** $\chi^2(n)$ with $n$ degrees of freedom is the distribution of the sum of squares of $n$ independent standard [[Normal Distribution|normal]] variables.

requirements.statement: For a normal random sample, (n-1)S^2/sigma^2 is chi-squared with n-1 degrees of freedom, because replacing mu with the sample mean costs one degree of freedom.
requirements.concept: Sample Variance Distribution for Normal Samples

places.quote: **Normal samples:** for a sample of size $n$ from $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with [[Sample Variance|sample variance]] $S^2$, $(n - 1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2(n - 1)$.
The divisor $n - 1$ is the **degrees of freedom**: one is spent estimating $\mu$ by $\bar{X}$, and the deviations $X_i - \bar{X}$ sum to zero, so only $n-1$ of them are free

requirements.statement: For a normal random sample, the sample mean is N(mu, sigma^2/n), so n(Xbar - mu)^2/sigma^2 is the square of a standard normal and is chi-squared with 1 degree of freedom.
requirements.concept: Sampling Distributions from a Normal Population

places.quote: The **Chi-Squared Distribution** $\chi^2(n)$ with $n$ degrees of freedom is the distribution of the sum of squares of $n$ independent standard [[Normal Distribution|normal]] variables.
For a Normal population the result is exact: $\bar{X} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$, and $\bar{X}$ is independent of the [[Sample Variance]] $S^2$

requirements.statement: For a normal random sample, the sample mean and the sample variance are independent.
requirements.concept: Sampling Distributions from a Normal Population

places.quote: For Normal data, $(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}$ independent of $\bar{X}$
For a Normal population the result is exact: $\bar{X} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)$, and $\bar{X}$ is independent of the [[Sample Variance]] $S^2$

requirements.statement: A t distribution with k degrees of freedom is the distribution of Z / sqrt(W/k), where Z is standard normal and W is an independent chi-squared with k degrees of freedom.

places.quote: **Student's t-Distribution** $t(n)$ with $n$ degrees of freedom is the distribution of a standard [[Normal Distribution|normal]] variable divided by the square root of an independent [[Chi-Squared Distribution|chi-squared]] variable over its degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: An F distribution with (m, k) degrees of freedom is the distribution of the ratio (U/m)/(V/k) of independent chi-squared variables U and V with m and k degrees of freedom.

places.quote: The **F-Distribution** $F(n, m)$ with $n$ numerator and $m$ denominator degrees of freedom is the distribution of the ratio of two independent [[Chi-Squared Distribution|chi-squared]] variables, each divided by its degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: The square of a t(k) random variable has an F(1, k) distribution.

places.quote: **Link to F:** $T^2 \sim F(1, n)$, so a two-sided t-test on one coefficient is the [[F-Distribution|F-test]] with one numerator degree of freedom.
**Link to t:** if $T \sim t(m)$ then $T^2 \sim F(1, m)$ — see [[Student's t-Distribution]].

requirements.statement: The likelihood ratio test of nested GLMs (with known dispersion) uses the drop in deviance between the smaller and larger model as the test statistic, scaled by dispersion when it is not 1.

places.quote: For [[Generalized Linear Model|GLMs]] this is the drop in [[Deviance|deviance]] divided by the [[Dispersion Parameter|dispersion parameter]].

For a GLM this statistic is the **difference in deviances divided by the dispersion**, $-2\ln\Lambda = (D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}})/\phi$, with $D$ the unscaled deviance and $\phi$ the [[Dispersion Parameter]] (equivalently, the difference in scaled deviances).
**Analysis of Deviance**: for nested models, $\dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\phi} \approx \chi^2_{\Delta p}$ when $\phi$ is known (large samples).

requirements.statement: Under the null hypothesis that the smaller nested model is adequate, the likelihood ratio statistic follows a chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the number of additional parameters in the larger model.

places.quote: for nested models with $p_1 < p_2$ parameters, $-2\ln\lambda = 2(\ell_2 - \ell_1)$ is approximately $\chi^2(p_2 - p_1)$ in large samples.
$r$ is the number of **restrictions** — the difference in free parameters between the full and reduced models — and the $\chi^2$ approximation is asymptotic (Wilks' theorem)
**Analysis of Deviance**: for nested models, $\dfrac{D_{\text{reduced}} - D_{\text{full}}}{\phi} \approx \chi^2_{\Delta p}$ when $\phi$ is known (large samples).

requirements.statement: A categorical predictor with k levels contributes k-1 parameters (dummy variables) because one level is the base level.

places.quote: A categorical predictor with $k$ levels is represented using $k-1$ **indicator (dummy) variables**; the omitted level is the **reference level**, absorbed into the intercept (see [[Parameter Estimate Tables]])
a nominal [[Categorical Predictor|categorical predictor]] with $k$ levels gets $k - 1$ indicator columns

requirements.statement: An interaction between two categorical predictors with k and m levels adds (k-1)(m-1) parameters.

To get a p-value from a chi-squared table, locate the test statistic between two tabulated critical values in the row for the degrees of freedom; the p-value lies between the corresponding upper-tail probabilities (1 minus the cumulative probabilities).

places.quote: Because $9.4$ also exceeds $9.35$ but not $11.34$ (the $0.990$ column), the [[p-Value|p-value]] lies between 0.01 and 0.025.

requirements.statement: For a Student's t-distribution with n degrees of freedom, n > 2, the variance is n/(n-2).

places.quote: $$\text{Var}(T) = \frac{n}{n - 2}, \quad n > 2$$

requirements.statement: The variance of a t-distribution exists only when degrees of freedom exceed 2, and the mean is 0 (for df > 1).

In a linear regression with p predictors plus an intercept fitted to n observations, the residual degrees of freedom are n - p - 1, and the t-statistic for a coefficient is compared to a t distribution with these degrees of freedom.

places.quote: in simple [[Linear Regression|linear regression]], $t = \hat{\beta}_1/\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_1)$ has a $t(n - 2)$ distribution when $\beta_1 = 0$

a [[Linear Regression|linear regression]] table reports **t-values** — $\sigma^2$ is estimated from the residuals, so under Normal errors $\hat\beta_j/\text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$ follows a $t$ distribution with $n-p-1$ degrees of freedom ($p$ predictors plus an intercept)

requirements.statement: The p-value of a t-test is the probability, under the null hypothesis, of observing a t-statistic at least as extreme as the one observed; for a two-sided alternative it uses both tails of the t distribution.

places.quote: A **p-Value** is the probability, computed assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one obtained.
$$\text{p-value} = P(\text{test statistic as extreme or more extreme} \mid H_0 \text{ true})$$

requirements.statement: To bound a p-value using a t table, find the row for the degrees of freedom, locate the two critical values that bracket the absolute t-statistic, and read off the corresponding tail-area range.
